## Psalms - Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_rx9u)

Introduction to Psalms
======================

Part 1: General Introduction
----------------------------

### Outline of Psalms

1. Book One (Psalms 1–41\): Psalms of David
2. Book Two (Psalms 42–72\): Mostly psalms of David
3. Book Three (Psalms 73–89\): Psalms of Asaph, the Korahites, Ethan
4. Book Four (Psalms 90–106\): Mostly anonymous psalms
5. Book Five (Psalms 107–150\): Mostly anonymous, several psalms of David

### What is the book of Psalms?

The book of Psalms is a collection of songs that are addressed to God or that speak about God. The word “psalm” comes from a Greek term that described a song that a person would sing while playing a stringed instrument. In many languages, the word now refers to the songs in this collection in the Bible. (All of the songs were written in Hebrew, but they are now called by a Greek name because at one point many Jews became speakers of Greek.) People often call the writers of these psalms “psalmists.”

### What title should translators use for this book?

Translators may use the traditional title of this book, “The Book of Psalms,” or just “Psalms.” Another possible title for this book is “Songs for Worship,” which expresses the meaning of the term “psalms” as it applies to the songs in this book. Translators may use a title that expresses that meaning in their own language, or they may choose to transliterate the term “psalms,” that is, to use that word and spell it the way it sounds in their own language.

### Why were the songs in this book written?

The psalmists composed these songs for a variety of reasons. In some psalms, they expressed their praise to God. In other psalms, they asked God for help and expressed confidence in his love and power. In still others, they confessed their sins and begged for mercy. The Israelites wrote some psalms to ask Yahweh to defeat their enemies. Other psalms celebrated the event of a new king beginning his reign. They wrote some psalms to instruct people on how to be wise by honoring Yahweh and obeying his law. Pilgrims sang some of the psalms while traveling to Jerusalem to worship there. Psalms written for all of these reasons became songs that people sang to worship Yahweh at his temple. Many songs that people found especially meaningful and enjoyable to sing in temple worship were collected together into this book, which has become part of the Bible.

### When were the songs in the book of Psalms written?

The psalms were written over a long period of time. Moses probably wrote the earliest psalm around 1400 B.C. David and Asaph wrote their psalms between 1020 and 975 B.C. The Korahites may have written their psalms before Jerusalem was destroyed and the Jews were exiled to Babylon in 587 B.C. Psalm 126 appears to come from the period after the exile, which ended in 538 B.C.

### Why do some versions number the psalms differently from others?

From ancient times, people have numbered the psalms in different ways. The Jews numbered the psalms in Hebrew in one way. When the psalms were translated into Greek, they were numbered in a different way. Also, the people who compiled and transmitted the book of Psalms seem to have wanted a round number of 150 psalms, and they divided and combined individual psalms in order to achieve that total. This was done in different ways in different versions. For example, in the traditional Hebrew text, Psalms 42 and 43 are presented as separate psalms while Psalm 116 is presented as a single psalm. In the ancient Greek version, Psalms 42 and 43 are a single psalm and Psalm 116 is presented in parts as two different psalms. The Hebrew and Greek numbering and the divisions and combinations of some psalms were passed down through the centuries, and a variety of systems are in use today. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the system that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the system that the ULT uses.

Part 2: Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Book
----------------------------------------------------

Most of the psalms were written in one of a few basic forms that were common in ancient Hebrew songwriting. These forms allowed the biblical songwriters to structure a creative expression of the powerful emotions and intense spiritual sensations that arose from their deep experiences with God. Psalmists used specific forms for specific purposes.

Notes to individual psalms will suggest what form they use. (Some psalms combine or adapt the basic forms.) Recognizing from the form the type of situation that the psalmist was addressing will help translators understand and appreciate each psalm as a whole in order to translate it effectively into their language.

### Psalms of supplication (laments)

The most common type of psalm in this collection is a plea for God’s help in a time of trouble. About one third of the psalms fit this type. These are often called “psalms of supplication” or “laments.” Many begin with a cry for help. The psalmist calls out to God, begging for rescue in urgent and emotional tones. The psalmist may then describe the troubles he is experiencing, but he may also make a statement of trust, expressing his confidence in God’s goodness and power despite these difficulties. He may ask God to do something specific to help him. He may say that God should do this because he is innocent of any wrongdoing. He may promise to praise God publicly once he has received his help. Not every psalm of supplication has all of these elements, and the elements that are present may appear in a variety of orders. Nevertheless, in these psalms of supplication, there is a recognizable basic pattern of calling for help from a standpoint of trust.

### Psalms of thanksgiving

People who had promised to praise God publicly for his help sang another kind of psalm in order to do that. Those psalms are often called “psalms of thanksgiving.” They too are composed from a number of common elements. There may be an opening summary statement that God helped the psalmist when he was in trouble. The psalmist may call others to join him in praising God for this. He may describe the trouble he was in and state specifically that he asked God to help him. He may then depict, often through vivid imagery, how God helped him, and he may conclude with an expression of praise and thanks. Once again, not every psalm of thanksgiving has all of these elements, and the elements that are present may appear in a variety of orders, but a basic pattern is recognizable.

### Psalms of praise

The third basic type of song in this book is often called a “psalm of praise.” Its focus is not on the writer and his situation but on God and his worthiness to be worshiped. In a psalm of praise, the writer calls other people to worship God with him, and he gives reasons why they should do that. The essential dynamic of psalms of praise is alternation between calls to worship and reasons to worship (though some of them consist almost entirely of a call to worship). A reason to worship is typically introduced with the term “for.” Psalm 47:5–6 say, for example, “Sing praise to our king, sing praise! For God is the king of all of the earth.” One particular type of praise psalm is a “song of Zion,” which celebrates Mount Zion and the city of Jerusalem and the temple there as the center of God’s presence and rule over the earth.

### Psalms of trust

A psalmist may sometimes expand one element of a basic form so that it fills all or most of a psalm. For example, psalmists who asked God for help often expressed their trust in him. Some psalms consist almost entirely of an expression of trust. The troubles of the psalmist may be dimly perceptible in the background, but these psalms are essentially calm, stately affirmations of reliance on God. They are therefore called “psalms of trust.”

### Penitential psalms

Sometimes a psalmist recognizes that the trouble that he is experiencing is the result of sin that he has committed. In addition to difficulties that are consequences of his sin or punishments for it, he is deeply troubled by guilt. He asks God to forgive him and restore him. Expressing sorrow for doing wrong is sometimes called “penitence,” and so such psalms are sometimes called “penitential psalms.” They are a specific kind of psalm of supplication.

### Imprecatory psalms

Sometimes psalmists who are troubled by wicked enemies become concerned not only for their own survival but for God’s reputation for upholding justice. If treacherous people succeed and prosper, others may question whether God is good and powerful enough to vindicate the righteous and punish the wicked. Those others may then choose to act wickedly themselves, and the entire society will become violent and corrupt. So a psalm of supplication for deliverance from enemies may include a call for God to destroy the wicked. That kind of request is sometimes called an “imprecation.” When this call expands and becomes the major element of a composition, that psalm may be called an “imprecatory psalm.” Christian readers of such psalms, knowing that Jesus told his followers to love their enemies, are often troubled by the call for God to destroy wicked people. It is important to appreciate that psalmist is not asking for revenge. He is asking God to demonstrate his justice.

### Wisdom psalms

Some psalms make a practical application of the truth about God’s justice. They teach their listeners about the two very different fates that await wicked people and righteous people. These psalms urge their audiences to cultivate wisdom (the ability to choose the right course in life) by fearing God, that is, by having great reverence for God and obeying him. While some wisdom psalms present their teaching within the framework of one of the basic types, other wisdom psalms are different. They are addressed to people, rather than to God, and they consist essentially of teaching rather than of supplication, thanksgiving, or praise. One type of psalm that is similar to a wisdom psalm depicts God assembling and addressing the Israelites, commending those who are faithfully obeying his covenant but warning those who are acting wickedly.

### Royal psalms

God’s power and goodness can be questioned in a psalm of supplication, vindicated in a psalm of thanksgiving, and celebrated in a psalm of praise. Some praise psalms celebrate how God is enthroned as king above all the earth and how, from that position of authority, he exercises his power on behalf of justice and helps needy people. The description of God’s enthronement as a reason to worship can expand to fill an entire psalm of praise. When it does, the psalm may be known as a “divine enthronement psalm” or “royal psalm.” Another type of royal psalm is a prayer for God to help the Israelite king uphold justice and help needy people as God’s representative on earth. This type of royal psalm, a specific kind of psalm of supplication, may also ask God to defeat the king’s foreign enemies so that he can continue to rule. Some such psalms celebrate the occasion of a new king beginning his rule.

### Styles of psalms

The background information that the book of Psalms provides about many of the songs in this collection (see the discussion of “superscriptions” in Part 3 of this introduction) sometimes includes a description of the style of a psalm.

In several cases, a psalm is identified as a “maskil.” Biblical scholars have different understandings of what that term means. Some say it means “to instruct,” while others say that the word refers to the skill used in creating the psalm. Still others think it means that meditation should be used in reading this psalm. Since the meaning is not certain, in your translation, you may wish to represent this word in its Hebrew form, as the ULT and UST do, and spell it the way it sounds in your language.

In several other cases, a psalm is identified as a “miktam.” The exact meaning of this term is also uncertain. Some scholars think it may refer to a kind of writing or musical style, while others suggest it describes the psalm’s tone or purpose. It may mean that a psalm is a prayer for protection or a song of confidence. Since the meaning is not certain, you may wish to represent this word as well in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language.

Fifteen short psalms, collected together as Psalms 120–134, are each called a “song of ascents.” Most interpreters understand this title to mean that they were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for the great festivals of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. (The term “ascents” is used because going up to Jerusalem involved a climb of about 3,000 feet up Mount Zion.) These songs are written in a variety of forms, and while many of them refer directly to the journey and the festivals, they also speak about a broad range of other experiences. So this description refers as much to the occasion of these psalms as their style, although they are generally short and communal.

Several of the psalms follow a pattern in which the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet begin each poetic line, each half\-line, every second line, or even every eight lines in a row. This pattern is known as an “acrostic,” from a Greek term that describes the start of a line of poetry. The alphabetic pattern may be used as an aid to memory, and it may also depict a composition as speaking comprehensively about a subject. The background information that the book of Psalms provides does not identify these psalms as having been written in this style, since this would have been obvious to the original Hebrew audience, but notes to these psalms will identify them as acrostics.

Part 3: Translation Issues in This Book
---------------------------------------

### How should translators represent the poetry in the book of Psalms?

The psalms, as the words to songs, are poetry. Hebrew poetry was based on the repetition of ideas. Typically the first part of a line would say something, and the second part of that line would repeat the same idea in different words. (In some cases, the second part of a line may elaborate on the idea in the first part or state something contrasting.) Translation teams must decide how to represent the lines in which both parts express the same idea. Readers may think that the psalmist is saying something different in the second part of the line but not be able to figure out what that is, since the psalmist is actually not doing that. So one approach is to combine the two parts into a single statement of the idea. However, to show readers the character of Hebrew poetry, it may be preferable to include both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. (This can be valuable in many cases because the second part, while restating the idea, often advances or intensifies it in some way.) Often the term “and” connects the two parts, and it may be clearer in your language to connect them with a different term in order to show that the second part of the line is repeating the idea in the first part, not saying something different. For example, Psalm 19:1 says, “The heavens are declaring the glory of God, and the sky is proclaiming the work of his hands.” A translation might say, “The heavens are declaring the glory of God; indeed, the sky is proclaiming the work of his hands.”

Translation teams must also decide whether to try to represent the poetry in the Psalms in a poetic form that is characteristic of their own language. This is often difficult to do, since poetic forms vary so much from one language to another. Unless poetry in the translators’ language happens to be very similar to Hebrew poetry, a common approach is to represent the psalms as prose, that is, as ordinary language, but to format them in a way that shows they are poetry in the original language. The ULT and UST do that by setting each line farther to the right on the page than regular text. They indent the second part of a line (and a third part, if there is one) farther to the right than the first part of the line. Translators may have conventions in their own languages and cultures that will allow them to translate the psalms as ordinary language but display them as poetry.

However translation teams decide to represent the poetry in the Psalms, it is valuable to retain the images that the psalmists use, such as God being like a shepherd or like a huge rock. These images reflect the original cultural and historical context of the Bible, which is helpful background for readers to have in order to understand what the Bible is saying. In many cases the images are used in various parts of the Bible with similar meaning but significant shades of difference, and it is helpful for readers to see how the biblical writers are using images in these different ways. So if an image communicates well in your language, please use it in your translation. If not, consider expressing it as a comparison. For example, for the statement in Psalm 23:1, “Yahweh is my shepherd,” you might say, “Yahweh cares for me as a shepherd cares for his sheep.” For the statement in Psalm 18:2, “Yahweh is my rock,” you might say, “Yahweh to me is like a high rock that I can climb up to reach safety from danger.”

### How should translators represent the introductions that many psalms have?

In many cases, information about a psalm is provided before the beginning of the psalm. This information is sometimes called a “superscription.” That term describes something that is written above something else.

Some versions do not give verse numbers to the superscriptions, while other versions do. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to do what it does. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to do what the ULT does. Whether or not translators give the superscriptions in the Psalms verse numbers, they should consider them as part of the divinely inspired biblical text. They may wish to use special formatting to show that they are not part of the original composition of the psalm. The ULT does this by putting them in italics.

Translators should use care in translating the phrases in superscriptions that associate a psalm with a person. For example, about half of the psalms are called a “psalm of David” or simply “Of David.” This may mean that King David wrote them. However, it could also mean that someone else wrote the psalm for David, or that the psalm was written in the same style that David used when he wrote songs. Translators can be more confident that this expression means that David wrote the psalm when the superscription describes a historical situation in David’s life as the occasion of its composition. The UST models various ways to translate the phrases that associate a psalm with a person, sometimes with expressions that could allow a range of meanings (“A psalm of David”) and sometimes with more specific expressions (“David wrote this psalm when …”).

Some superscriptions give instructions about how a psalm should be played and sung. They may tell which instruments, singers, or melodies should be used for that psalm. The superscriptions to about a third of the psalms indicate that they are “for the chief musician.” This suggests that while they were originally composed in a variety of life situations, they have been collected for use in temple worship. The ULT and UST model how the technical terms in the superscription about performance can be translated in either a form\-based or meaning\-based way.

Some biblical scholars suggest that these musical instructions apply to the previous psalm rather than to the psalm that immediately follows them. For example, the current superscription to Psalm 4 reads, “For the director, with stringed instruments. Of David.” The phrases “For the chief musician; with stringed instruments” may belong at the end of Psalm 3, so that the superscription to Psalm 4 would be just “Of David.” Similarly, the superscription to Psalm 5 may be just “A psalm of David,” and the musical instructions “For the chief musician; on the flutes” may belong at the end of Psalm 4\. This suggestion is a matter of ongoing scholarly debate, and Bible publishers have so far not adopted it, so these resources treat the entire traditional superscriptions as applying to the psalms that immediately follow them. However, you may wish to consider the merits of this suggestion and make your own decision about it as a translation team.

### “Selah” and “Higgaion”

The terms “Selah” and “Higgaion” occur within many psalms. They seem to be musical terms inserted as directions for singers and musicians. Scholars do not agree as to their exact meaning. For this reason, rather than try to translate them, translators may decide to include the Hebrew words and spell them the way they sound in their language or leave them out.

### How should translators represent passages in the psalms that look forward to the Messiah?

New Testament writers quote many passages from the psalms as prophecies about the Messiah, Jesus Christ. The psalms that contain these prophecies are therefore sometimes called “Messianic psalms.” In translating them, translators should take care not to limit the potential meaning only to the original writer. For example, David says in Psalm 16:10, “You will not hand over your godly one to see the pit.” In speaking to Yahweh, he is referring initially to himself in the third person as “your godly one.” In some languages, a speaker would not refer to himself in the third person in this way, and translators of the Bible into those languages might ordinarily use an expression such as “me, your godly one.” However, Peter cites this statement in Acts 2:27 as a prophecy of the Messiah. So it would be preferable to translate the phrase “your godly one” with a phrase such as “any godly person who belongs to you.”

### “shall”

The ULT represents the Hebrew instructional verb form with the English helping verb “shall.” For example, when Yahweh said, as quoted by Asaph in 81:9, “There shall not be a strange god among you.” he was instructing the Israelites how to act. Other ways to say this are “You are not to have a strange god among you,” “You should not have a strange god among you” “I want you not to have a strange god among you,” or “Do not have a strange god among you.” Translate this form with the most natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### “let” and “may”

The ULT uses the English helping verbs “let” and “may” to show that a speaker is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. It uses the verb “let” for more assertive expressions, and it uses the verb “may” for more deferential expressions. For example, when David says in 69:34 “Let the heavens and the earth praise him,” he means “I want the heavens and the earth to praise him.” Languages that do not have a volitional form might say “The heavens and earth ought to praise him,” or they might use an imperative, “Praise him, heavens and earth!” When David says in 70:5 “Yahweh, may you not delay,” he is being more deferential, even though his wish is urgent, because he is addressing a superior. Languages that do not have a volitional form might say “Yahweh, I desire that you do not delay,” or they might use an imperative with an indication that it is a polite request, “Yahweh, please do not delay.” Translate this volitional form in the most natural way in your language to indicate that the speaker is expressing what he wants someone to do or what he wishes someone would do.

### “your God,” “my God,” and “our God”

Throughout this book, the psalmist refers to Yahweh with possessive forms such as “your God,” “my God,” and “our God.” By using these possessive forms, he is not saying that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. Also, when the psalmist says, “your God,” he is referring to the same God that he also worships. He is not distinguishing between the God of the Israelites and his own God.

## Psalms - Chapter 1 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_fan4)

Psalm 1 Introduction
====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 1 is usually considered to be a “wisdom psalm,” which gives advice to those who hear it read or sung.

1. The happy: Those devoted to Yahweh’s instruction prosper (1–3\)
2. The unhappy: Those who reject Yahweh’s instruction come to nothing (4–5\)
3. Authority: Yahweh directs each path to its destination (6\)

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: to celebrate the one who follows Yahweh’s guidance
2. Content: It is the one who delights in Yahweh’s guidance who is “happy.” All of this is because Yahweh cares for righteous people, but wicked people keep sinning until Yahweh destroys them forever. (6\)
3. Message: Devotion to Yahweh’s guidance leads to success and honor.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

1. Words associated (whether by sound or by meaning) with a journey appear throughout the psalm.
2. In Hebrew, in the word “wicked” the consonant sounds in “happy” are reversed.
3. Verses 1 and 5 have a number of correspondences with one another. There are negated clauses in both verses, and both contain motion verbs. Additionally, the phrase “advice of the wicked” in verse 1a is similar to the phrase “congregation of the righteous” in verse 5b. The phrases also have similar structure. In Hebrew the words for “advice” and “congregation” sound very similar. See: Poetry
4. The psalm begins and ends with the metaphor of a journey.
5. There is agricultural imagery which is frequent in scripture: a tree by water (representing flourishing through God’s blessing) and separating wheat from chaff (representing the different judgments of the righteous and wicked). See: Biblical Imagery — Extended Metaphors

אַ֥שְֽׁרֵי

**"The happinesses of"**

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, what constitutes true happiness from God’s perspective. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: \[Oh, how happy is]

## Psalms 1:1 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_n9y3)

אַ֥שְֽׁרֵי־הָ⁠אִ֗ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֤ר ׀ לֹ֥א הָלַךְ֮ בַּ⁠עֲצַ֪ת רְשָׁ֫עִ֥ים וּ⁠בְ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ חַ֭טָּאִים לֹ֥א עָמָ֑ד וּ⁠בְ⁠מוֹשַׁ֥ב לֵ֝צִ֗ים לֹ֣א יָשָֽׁב

**"The happinesses of the man who walks not in the advice of the wicked, and stands not in the pathway of sinners, and sits not in the seat of scoffers"**

In some languages it may be more natural to place the declaration of the state of the man at the end of the verse after the description of the characteristics that he avoids. However, starting the psalm with the **happinesses of the man** was an intentional poetic decision by the author, who intended to set the mood of the psalm. Translators should consider how their language might start the psalm in this way. Alternate translation: \[The man who does not walk in the advice of the wicked ones, and stands not in the pathway with sinners, and sits not in the seat of mockers is happy.]

See: Information Structure

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 1:1

**"walks not in the advice of the wicked"**

## Psalms 1:1 (#6) (id: en_tn_PSA_x0do)

לֹ֥א הָלַךְ֮ בַּ⁠עֲצַ֪ת רְשָׁ֫עִ֥ים וּ⁠בְ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ חַ֭טָּאִים לֹ֥א עָמָ֑ד וּ⁠בְ⁠מוֹשַׁ֥ב לֵ֝צִ֗ים לֹ֣א יָשָֽׁב

**"walks not in the advice of the wicked, and stands not in the pathway of sinners, and sits not in the seat of scoffers"**

It may be helpful to read these three phrases in an inverted way. That way the negative trajectory that the happy man avoids can be more clearly seen. Consider: “Unhappy is the man who walks in the advice of the wicked ones and then who stands in the pathway of sinners and then who sits in the seat of scoffers.” The meaning of each of these parts of this extended metaphor is expanded in later notes, but translators should see a trajectory of worsening character that a happy man avoids.

See: Biblical Imagery — Extended Metaphors

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 1:1
* **Associated Articles:** Biblical Imagery — Extended Metaphors (ID: `33272@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** To Sin (ID: `keyterm:Sin`); Counsel (ID: `keyterm:Counsel`)

## Psalms 1:1 (#7) (id: en_tn_PSA_y9ow)

וּ⁠בְ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ חַ֭טָּאִים לֹ֥א עָמָ֑ד

**"and stands not in the pathway of sinners"**

The **pathway** means how a person lives his life. Not only does the happy man not do what the wicked say but he habitually avoids doing what sinners do. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the comparison. Alternate translation: \[and does not stand with sinners in the path of sinning] or \[and does not make sinning a habit]

וְֽ⁠הָיָ֗ה כְּ⁠עֵץ֮ שָׁת֪וּל עַֽל־פַּלְגֵ֫י מָ֥יִם אֲשֶׁ֤ר פִּרְי֨⁠וֹ ׀ יִתֵּ֬ן בְּ⁠עִתּ֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠עָלֵ֥⁠הוּ לֹֽא־יִבּ֑וֹל וְ⁠כֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁר־יַעֲשֶׂ֣ה יַצְלִֽיחַ

**"And he is like a tree set to grow by streams of water, which gives its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither, and he makes successful all that he does"**

The point of this verse’s comparison between the happy man and a well\-watered tree is that just like the streams of water cause the tree to flourish, learning Yahweh’s instructions causes the man to flourish. (In the original, the phrases even sound similar.) Both a positive and negative comparison are given to strengthen the force of the point. The tree, fruit, and leaf references connect both back to Eden and forward to the end of Revelation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the argument a little more explicit as the “Like … so” connection does in the UST. See 92:12–92:14 for another use of this imagery.

See: Simile

## Psalms 1:4 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_as72)

כַּ֝⁠מֹּ֗ץ

**"they are} like \& chaff"**

The word **chaff** refers to the parts of a wheat or other grain plant that are not food. The husk that surrounds the edible seed is very light, and it blows away when the wheat is threshed to separate out the edible seed. Thus, the chaff is with the grain until harvest but then separated and blown away. If your readers would not be familiar with the word **chaff** you could use a more general term or use another light and worthless material to describe the wicked. Alternate translation: \[they are like … dried seed husks] or \[they are like … fallen]

## Psalms - Chapter 2 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_z14u)

Psalm 2 Introduction
====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 2 is usually considered a royal psalm because it is about the king.

1. Rebellion: Earthly kings plot rebellion (1–3\)
2. Response: The Heavenly King laughs (4–6\)
3. Decree: The King on Zion recounts Yahweh’s covenant (7–9\)
4. Ultimatum: Earthly kings, “Serve Yahweh … Kiss the son!” (10–12\)

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: It was probably first sung when a new person became the king.
2. Content: While there are (from the perspective of the New Testament) clear references to Jesus, the Anointed (Messiah) Son of God (Yahweh), translators should avoid bringing this fuller understanding into the translation of this psalm, which was written around 1,000 years before Christ.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

1. The place of reference moves between things being on earth (2\), in heaven (4\), on the mountain (often seen as a meeting place between heaven and earth) (6\), and on earth again (10\).
2. The rebellious words in verse 3 are echoed by similar sounding but very contrastive (obedient) words in verses 10–12\.
3. The word for son in verse 12 is highlighted by being Aramaic rather than Hebrew and having several occurrences of similar sounding consonant groups near it. See: Poetry
4. Nations are personified.
5. Yahweh’s rule is pictured as physical bonds.
6. Power is figured as an iron rod.
7. Nations are figured as pottery.

### CCBYSA

Significant portions of the ULT, UST, and TNs for this psalm are derivative from “Psalms, Layer by Layer” (https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/Welcome), “Psalm 2” (https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/Psalm\_2\) by Cambridge Digital Bible Research, Katie Frost, Meaghan Smith, Nikki Mustin et al, used under CC BY

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 2:0
* **Associated Articles:** Poetry (ID: `33422@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 2:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_e4gn)

לָ֭⁠מָּה רָגְשׁ֣וּ גוֹיִ֑ם וּ֝⁠לְאֻמִּ֗ים יֶהְגּוּ־רִֽיק

**"Why do nations conspire and peoples plot futilely"**

The proper understanding of the questions that make up this verse is provided in verses 4 and those that follow. They are not true questions; they are statements of mocking disbelief. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate this as a statement or an exclamation. ## Psalms 2:2 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ag3k)

יִ֥תְיַצְּב֨וּ ׀ מַלְכֵי־אֶ֗רֶץ וְ⁠רוֹזְנִ֥ים נֽוֹסְדוּ־יָ֑חַד

**"The kings of the earth take their stand, and the rulers conspire together"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[The kings of the earth take their stand; indeed, the rulers conspire together]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms 2:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_bvs1)

נְֽ֭נַתְּקָה אֶת־מֽוֹסְרוֹתֵ֑י⁠מוֹ וְ⁠נַשְׁלִ֖יכָה מִמֶּ֣⁠נּוּ עֲבֹתֵֽי⁠מוֹ

**"Let us tear apart their bonds and cast their cords away from us"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Let us tear apart their bonds; truly, let us cast their cords away from us.]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 2:3
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Rope (ID: `realia:Rope`)

וַ֭⁠אֲנִי נָסַ֣כְתִּי

**"I, I have poured out"**

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will cut** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how significant it was that it was he and not someone else who was setting up this king on Zion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: \[I alone have poured out]

## Psalms - Chapter 3 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_py7j)

Psalm 3 Introduction
====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

1. Foes “rising” against psalmist (1–2\)
2. Trust expressed to Yahweh (on his holy hill, see 2:6\) (3–4\)
3. Trust in Yahweh proclaimed (5–6\)
4. Help petitioned from Yahweh (“rising” and saving refer back to 1–2\) (7–8\)

See 2 Samuel 15–18 for the story of David fleeing from Absalom.

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: to pray for salvation from enemies
2. Content: Yahweh, save me! My enemies are many, but you are my defense.
3. Message: Salvation is of Yahweh

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

1. The psalm divides into four sections that are nearly the same length (14 words / 14 words / 14 words / 15 words).
2. The second and third sections share similar beginnings; both begin with an independent personal pronoun (3a: “you;” 5a: “I”). “You” (\=Yahweh) is the topic of the second section (3–4\), and “I” (\=David) is the topic of the third section (5–6\).
3. The first section (1–2\) and the two middle sections (3–6\) are connected by the ideas of “many/multitudes … against me.” See: Poetry
4. Yahweh is pictured as a shield.
5. Safety is pictured as sleeping.
6. Yahweh’s salvation from enemies is pictured in violent graphic language.
7. Wicked people’s power is represented by their teeth.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

1. Selah: This psalm contains the first instances of the Hebrew word “Selah.” Refer to the introduction to Psalms for more information.
2. Superscriptions: This psalm is the first one which starts with a superscription. Refer to the introduction to Psalms for more information.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 3:0
* **Associated Articles:** Poetry (ID: `33422@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); Absalom (ID: `person:Absalom`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 3:2 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_oya5)

**"Selah"**

This is the first instance of the Hebrew word **Selah**, the meaning of which is unknown. כְּ֝בוֹדִ֗⁠י

**"my glory"**

Because Yahweh is the actor in all the other actions in this verse, calling **Yahweh** his **glory** probably means that Yahweh gives the psalmist glory or honor. Since the psalmist has just spoken about his enemies and about Yahweh being his protector, he probably means that Yahweh gives him glory by giving him victory over his enemies. ## Psalms 3:5 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_tup6)

אֲנִ֥י שָׁכַ֗בְתִּי וָֽ⁠אִ֫ישָׁ֥נָ⁠ה הֱקִיצ֑וֹתִי כִּ֖י יְהוָ֣ה יִסְמְכֵֽ⁠נִי

**"I laid myself down and slept. I awoke, for Yahweh protects me"**

The phrase **laid myself down and slept** is not a one\-time occurrence but a universal statement about his daily peace because of Yahweh. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases since the second phrase, **for Yahweh protects me**, gives the reason for the result, **I awoke** as well as the reason for the author’s confidence that he can lie down and sleep. Alternate translation: \[Because Yahweh protects me, I lie down, sleep, and awake]

See: Connect — Reason\-and\-Result Relationship

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 3:5
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship (ID: `33331@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 4 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_b2qk)

Psalm 4 Introduction
====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

1. Distress (1\)
2. Rebuke (2–6\)
3. Blessing (7–8\)

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: to intercede for the people and call them to repentance
2. Content: People, trust in Yahweh alone! He has relieved our suffering in the past, and he will help us again when I call to him. Yahweh, shine on us!
3. Message: Yahweh alone gives peace and security in times of distress.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

1. Features between verses 1, 6, and 8\. See the note in verse 6\.
2. Hebrew roots from verse 5 repeat in verses 7–9\. See the note in verse 5\.
3. There seems to be a morning and night pattern. The word translated **call** in verses 1 and 3 sound like the Hebrew word for morning, and then bed is mentioned in verse 4\. Yahweh lifting up the light of his face is like the dawn in verse 6 and in verse 8 the psalmist lies down to sleep.
4. The last verse of the psalm seems to wind down peacefully, even repeating “s” sounds. See the note in verse 8\.
See: Poetry

### CCBYSA

====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

1. Appeal (1–2\)
2. Precedent (3–7\)
3. Petition (8–11\)
4. Resolution (12\)

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: to petition the divine King and Judge for justice from enemies
2. Content: Yahweh, act justly! Banish the evildoers! Shelter the righteous!
3. Message: Yahweh is a just ruler, and he blesses the just.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

1. The first word of the content portion of the psalm starts with the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet and the final word starts with the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet. This symbolizes completeness; the author’s appeal to Yahweh is complete.
2. There is a parallel structure between verses 3–7 and verses 8–11:

A. Verses 3 and 8 start with an address to Yahweh, who is also the subject.

B. Verses 4 and 9 start with “For” followed by a word of negation. They use a verbless clause in Hebrew, and the wicked are the topic.

C. Verses 7 and 11 contrast with what is immediately before, and they speak of being with Yahweh.

D. There is also progression between each earlier verse and its related later verse either in specificity or time.
See: Poetry

## Psalms - Chapter 6 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_gpl3)

Psalm 6 Introduction
====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

1. Plea (1–5\)
2. Death (6–7\)
3. Answer (8–10\)

The psalm divides neatly in half between verses 5 and 6 with 34 words in each. The first half divides into two parts, verses 1–2 and verses 4–5, which parallel each other in structure and content.

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: to plead for mercy and healing
2. Content: Yahweh have mercy and heal me, because I am near death, and no one can praise you in death.
3. Message: Yahweh’s loyalty to David is stronger than sin and death (30:6\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

1. The first section (1–3\) and the last section (8–10\) are parallel. Not only are they the same length (3 verses, 6 lines), but they are also similar in content and sounds. Structurally, the first section and the last section stand in a symmetrical relationship to one another. The parallels help to define the structure of the psalm.
2. The effect of the repetition in the last section is to highlight the complete resolution and reversal of the situation. David’s prayer has been heard, his question of “How long?” has been answered (“in an instant!”), and the deep dismay that he experienced is now imparted to his enemies on whom Yahweh’s punishment rightfully falls.
3. The second section (6–7\) stands out in a number of ways, including figurative language, line structure, use of rare words, alliteration, delay of information, word repetition, and use of similar\-sounding words. The effect is to draw attention to this section of the poem, wherein David, on the brink of death, reaches to the heights of poetic/rhetorical technique in order to express the depths of his suffering in a last\-ditch effort to persuade Yahweh to rescue him.
4. Yahweh’s name appears eight times throughout the psalm, but it is conspicuously absent from the second section (6–7\), which follows the Psalmist’s statement that “in death, there is no remembrance of you” (5a).
5. In verses 6–7, it is as though David has descended into the world of the dead, the place where Yahweh is neither named nor praised. It is a place of darkness (night) and associated with watery chaos (tears/swim/melt). In the last section (8–10\), David regains energy, confidence, and authority, and he proclaims Yahweh’s name three times, as though he has come back from the dead.
6. Almost every verse in this psalm displays parallelism. Verse 2 and the first line of verse 3 are a three\-part parallel while the last line of verse 3 and the first line of verse 4 seem to be the only lines not in a parallelism construction. While all these phrases mean basically the same thing with the second emphasizing the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words, Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. (See: Parallelism)

## Psalms - Chapter 7 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_zey1)

Psalm 7 Introduction
====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

1. Injustice Rejected (1–5\)
2. Justice Requested (6–9\)
3. Justice Expected (10–16\)
4. Justice Praised (17\)

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: to invoke justice from Yahweh towards both the righteous (specifically himself) and the wicked (false accusers)
2. Content: God is a righteous judge. He saves the upright, and he brings an end to the wicked’s violence.
3. Message: King Yahweh will see to it that the wicked receive their punishment and that the righteous are vindicated.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Heights and depths provide the structure of the Psalm.

1. The Psalmist is brought down (1–5\)
2. Yahweh goes up to the highest place (6–9\)
3. The enemies are brought down (10–16\)
4. Praise to the Most High God (17\)

### Other translation issues

1. There are a number of explicit and implicit references to Yahweh as both warrior and judge, which are both important functions of a king, especially King Yahweh—a metaphor that runs throughout the Psalms.
2. The subject in verses 12–16 is ambiguous; only the pronoun “he” is used (but it must be the wicked in verses 14–16\). The psalmist might have chosen to leave the participants grammatically ambiguous in this entire section to create tension in what is a prominent section of the psalm (which is it, Yahweh or the wicked?!), as well as to teach an important lesson in line with the meaning of this psalm: to be wicked is to bring death upon oneself, but Yahweh is the one who ensures the destruction. In the UST and notes, the most likely persons are identified.

### Cush the Benjamite

Note the superscription and the specific circumstances. There is no other reference to this incident in the Scriptures. But there are references to David being opposed by those of the tribe of Benjamin during the time he was serving King Saul.
See: Poetry

## Psalms 7:3–5 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_dpor)

In some languages, translating verses 3–5 might require a significant rearrangement to make the meaning clear. This section presents a hypothetical situation where the psalmist calls a potential curse onto himself. You might have to connect each hypothetical situation in verses 3–4 with a consequence in verse 5, or even put verse 5 before the hypotheticals. However, it is important to notice that both verses 3–4 and verse 5 build up to a greater level of tension, with the peak of this tension at the end of verse 5\. As you translate, try to capture this growing sense of hypothetical sin and its consequences, doing so in a way that feels natural to the poetic style of your language.

See: Poetry

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 7:3-5
* **Associated Articles:** Poetry (ID: `33422@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 7:3–5 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_x9fh)

אִם־עָשִׂ֣יתִי זֹ֑את אִֽם־יֶשׁ־עָ֥וֶל בְּ⁠כַפָּֽ⁠י׃ אִם־גָּ֭מַלְתִּי שֽׁוֹלְמִ֥⁠י רָ֑ע וָ⁠אֲחַלְּצָ֖⁠ה צוֹרְרִ֣⁠י רֵיקָֽם

**"if I have done this, if there is wrong on my hands,if I have repaid evil {to} one {who was at} peace with me, or senselessly rescued my adversary"**

The psalmist presents a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he is sure that the condition he describes is not true. He is making the case that he is not guilty. When translating, use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true (similar to how it is done in the UST). Be careful, though: if you choose to translate it as a statement of the opposite, as seen in an alternate translation, you will need to also change the wording in verse 5 to reflect this negation, as shown at the end of the provided example. Alternate translation: \[since I have not done this, and since there is no wrong on my hands, since I have not repaid evil to one who was at peace with me, or senselessly rescued my adversary, then do not]

See: Connect — Contrary to Fact Conditions

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 7:3-5
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Contrary to Fact Conditions (ID: `33325@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 7:14 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_boou)

יְחַבֶּל־אָ֑וֶן וְ⁠הָרָ֥ה עָ֝מָ֗ל וְ⁠יָ֣לַד שָֽׁקֶר

**"he is pregnant with wickedness, and he conceives trouble, and he births lies"**

These three phrases mean basically the same thing. The second and third emphasize the meaning by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the later phrases are repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[he who is pregnant with wickedness, who also conceives trouble, who even births lies]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 7:14
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Mischief (ID: `keyterm:Mischief`)

## Psalms - Chapter 8 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_rs24)

Psalm 8 Introduction
====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

1. Superscription
2. Introduction (1–2\)
3. Question (3–4\)
4. Answer (5–8\)
5. Closing (9\)

About the Psalm
---------------

1. Purpose: to praise Yahweh for his majesty throughout all the earth
2. Content: Your name is majestic in all the earth! You bestow your glory on the heavens above, and you bestow glory on weak humans below.
3. Message: Yahweh’s majesty is revealed in weakness.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

1. The psalm begins and ends with the exact same exclamation—this serves to point out the purpose of the psalm.
2. The psalm progresses from top to bottom several times.

A. In verse 1b–2 it goes from the heavens down to the weakest of humans.

B. Verses 3–4 again go down from the heavens to man.

C. Verses 5–8 move from the heavenly beings through man, who is exalted and crowned with glory as Yahweh’s representative ruler of all creation, and down and out into creation, moving away from man’s primary spheres of dominion (domestic animals) progressively outward.

1. There are many echoes of Genesis 1\. References include: the heavens as created by Yahweh’s fingers (3\), the animals as made by his hands (6\), the dominion of man over creation (6–8, see also Genesis 1:26\).
2. Magnificent, Majesty, Splendor, Glory: Yahweh gives his weak representative (humans) many of his glorious attributes, and humans rule for Yahweh.
See: Poetry

## Psalms 8:5 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_hx3s)

מֵ⁠אֱלֹהִ֑ים

**"from the heavenly beings"**

The Hebrew word here could mean: (1\) **heavenly beings**. This generic term encompasses any sort of supernatural being in the heavens that humans are slightly less than (like the heavenly court in Job 1\). (2\) God. The most common translation for this word is God. However, the psalmist is speaking to Yahweh in this psalm, so if he meant God here, it would make more sense for him to say, ‘from you.’ (3\) angels. The ancient Greek translation uses this option, but this Hebrew word does not seem to mean angels elsewhere. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

## Psalms - Chapter 9 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_zq96)

Psalm 9 Introduction
====================

Psalms 9–10 as One Psalm
------------------------

This psalm has a superscription, but Psalm 10 does not. This fact and the acrostic nature of the two psalms (lines start with consecutive letters of the alphabet) has led many scholars to believe these two psalms may have originally been written as one psalm. The analysis of the structure of these psalms presented here will assume that. It is recommended that you follow the versification and chapter structure of other Bibles you are familiar with.

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

The outlines for psalms 9 and 10 are combined here and in the introduction to psalm 10 because they were probably originally one psalm. Your translation will probably be best if you translate them together.

1. Psalm 9:1–10 Praise of the King
2. Psalm 9:11–20 Petition the King
3. Psalm 10:1–11 Persecution of the Poor
4. Psalm 10:12–18 Proclamation of the King

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Order and chaos

The first letter of many of the lines of these two psalms follows an acrostic (alphabetic) pattern. In some places, however, this orderly pattern is interrupted. The places where it is interrupted are places where the wicked are mentioned or acting. It is as if the presence of the wicked disrupts the orderliness over even the poetry, but it is restored and kept by Yahweh. If your language has a poetic style which can indicate order and chaos, you may wish to translate:

1. 9:1–4 in an orderly style
2. 9:5–6 in a slightly chaotic style
3. 9:7–15 in an orderly style
4. 9:16–17 in a slightly chaotic style
5. 9:18 in neither
6. 9:19–20 in an orderly style
7. 10:1 in an orderly style
8. 10:2–11 in a very chaotic style
9. 10:12–18 in an orderly style

### The fortress and the pit

There are two chiasms in psalm 9\. In the first half, Yahweh is compared to a fortress (9\) and, poetically, his judgment forms a barrier between the enemies and the psalmist and the oppressed.

1. people trust Yahweh (1–2\)
2. Yahweh is a judge (3–4\)
3. The enemy (5–6\)
4. Yahweh is a king and judge (7–8\)
5. People trust Yahweh (9–10\)

In the second half, people’s prayers poetically encircle the wicked, causing them to fall into their own pit.

1. People pray to Yahweh for help (especially verse 13\) (11–14\)
2. The wicked are destroyed by their own pit (15–18\)
3. People pray to Yahweh for help (19–20\)

As you translate this psalm, you will probably have a structure that matches this which may or may not be meaningful in your language. You could also consider if there is a way to poetically “surround” the wicked, with Yahweh as judge and the prayers of his people in the two sections.

### Adjectives used as generic nouns:

The adjectives “wicked, afflicted, innocent”, and “oppressed” are nominal adjectives used as generic nouns in these psalms. See Nominal Adjectives and Generic Noun Phrases. CCBYSA

## Psalms 9:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_lr4k)

בְּ⁠כָל־לִבִּ֑⁠י

**"with all my heart"**

Here the speaker is using one part, the **heart**, to represent the whole person. If another body part represents this in your culture, you could use it or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[with all my being] or \[with my whole person]

## Psalms 9:3–4 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_e4sg)

מִ⁠פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ׃ כִּֽי

**"from your face.For"**

## Psalms 9:4 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_bcg6)

**"you have done my justice and my claim"**

## Psalms 9:4 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_nvz1)

יָשַׁ֥בְתָּ לְ֝⁠כִסֵּ֗א

**"you have sat on your throne"**

Here, **throne** represents kingship. Kings had authority to judge people, and they would sit on their throne when they judged. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[you are like a king who judged his people from his throne] or \[you are a king]

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 9:4
* **Associated Articles:** Metonymy (ID: `33293@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 9:5 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_cw1j)

שְׁמָ֥⁠ם מָ֝חִ֗יתָ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֥ם וָ⁠עֶֽד

**"you blotted out their name forever and ever"**

This could mean: (1\) Yahweh caused these people to be forgotten. The end of verse 6 is parallel with this verse if you favor this interpretation. Alternate translation: \[you have caused them to be forgotten as if their name was blotted out] or \[no one will ever remember them again], (2\) Yahweh will not give these people eternal life (other parts of the Bible speak of this as blotting them out from the Book of Life). Alternate translation: \[you send them to eternal punishment]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 9:5
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 9:8 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_pgg5)

וְ⁠ה֗וּא יִשְׁפֹּֽט־תֵּבֵ֥ל בְּ⁠צֶ֑דֶק יָדִ֥ין לְ֝אֻמִּ֗ים בְּ⁠מֵישָׁרִֽים

**"as for him, he will judge the world with righteousness, and he will adjudicate for the peoples with fairness"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. Translate them according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information. Alternate translation: \[as for him, he will judge the world with righteousness, yes, he will adjudicate for the peoples with fairness] or \[as for him, he will judge the people of the world with righteousness and fairness]

## Psalms 9:17–18 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_qi1h)

Verses 17–18 form a poetic device called a chiasm where the inner two lines parallel each other and the outer two lines also parallel each other. In this case this artistic device creates a strong contrast between the verses by contrasting people forgetting God with God not forgetting the needy and contrasts the death of the wicked with the hope of the afflicted which does not die. If your language has a poetic structure that can make contrasts stand out markedly like this, consider using it here.

See: Poetry

## Psalms - Chapter 10 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_h366)

Psalm 10 Introduction
=====================

Psalms 9–10 as One Psalm
------------------------

Psalm 9 has a superscription but Psalm 10 does not. This fact and the acrostic nature of the two psalms (lines start with consecutive letters of the alphabet) has led many scholars to believe these two psalms may have originally been written as one psalm. The analysis of the structure of these psalms presented here will assume that. It is recommended that you follow the versification and chapter structure of other Bibles you are familiar with.

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

The outlines for psalms 9 and 10 are combined here and in the introduction to psalm 10 because they were probably originally one psalm. Your translation will probably be best if you translate them together.

1. Psalm 9:1–10 Praise of the King
2. Psalm 9:11–20 Petition the King
3. Psalm 10:1–11 Persecution of the poor
4. Psalm 10:12–18 Proclamation of the King

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Order and chaos

The first letter of many of the lines of these two psalms follows an acrostic (alphabetic) pattern. In some places, however, this orderly pattern is interrupted. The places where it is interrupted are places where the wicked are mentioned or acting. It is as if the presence of the wicked disrupts the orderliness over even the poetry, but it is restored and kept by Yahweh. If your language has a poetic style which can indicate order and chaos, you may wish to translate:

1. 9:1–4 in an orderly style
2. 9:5–6 in a slightly chaotic style
3. 9:7–15 in an orderly style
4. 9:16–17 in a slightly chaotic style
5. 9:18 in neither
6. 9:19–20 in an orderly style
7. 10:1 in an orderly style
8. 10:2–11 in a very chaotic style
9. 10:12–18 in an orderly style

### The fortress and the pit

There are two chiasms in psalm 9\. In the first half, Yahweh is compared to a fortress (9\) and, poetically, his judgment forms a barrier between the enemies and the psalmist and the oppressed.

1. People trust Yahweh (1–2\)
2. Yahweh is a judge (3–4\)
3. The enemy (5–6\)
4. Yahweh is a king and judge (7–8\)
5. People trust Yahweh (9–10\)

In the second half, people’s prayers poetically encircle the wicked, causing them to fall into their own pit.

1. People pray to Yahweh for help (especially verse 13\) (11–14\)
2. The wicked are destroyed by their own pit (15–18\)
3. People pray to Yahweh for help (19–20\)

As you translate this psalm, you will probably have a structure that matches this which may or may not be meaningful in your language. You could also consider if there is a way to poetically “surround” the wicked with the prayers of Yahweh’s people and with Yahweh as judge, in the two sections.

### Adjectives used as generic nouns:

The adjectives “wicked, afflicted, innocent”, and “oppressed” are nominal adjectives used as generic nouns in these psalms. See Nominal Adjectives and Generic Noun Phrases.
See: Poetry

## Psalms 10:2 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_ml6r)

יִתָּפְשׂ֓וּ ׀ בִּ⁠מְזִמּ֖וֹת ז֣וּ חָשָֽׁבוּ

**"may they be caught by the schemes that they have planned"**

It is not clear who **they** are. Options include: (1\) that **they** are the wicked in both cases. In that case this would either be a prediction or a wish. This would fit with what is said in 9:15–16\. Alternate translation: \[the wicked are caught by the schemes that they themselves have planned] or \[may the wicked be caught by the schemes that they themselves have planned] or (2\) the first **they** is the **afflicted** and the second is the **wicked**. This would fit with the very negative outlook of 10:1–11\. Alternate translation: \[the afflicted are caught by the schemes that the wicked have planned]. You may wish to follow the choice that translations you are familiar with have made.

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 10:2
* **Associated Articles:** Pronouns — When to Use Them (ID: `33424@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Plan (ID: `keyterm:Plan`)

## Psalms 10:3 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_wf55)

וּ⁠בֹצֵ֥עַ בֵּ֝רֵ֗ךְ נִ֘אֵ֥ץ ׀ יְהוָֽה

**"and he blesses the robber; he despises Yahweh"**

It is difficult to discern who is the subject and object of both verbs in the second half of this verse. Additionally, some believe that **blesses** is an euphemism for “curses” here. The ULT seeks to offer a reasonable translation where **the wicked** is the subject throughout (occurrences of **he** in the ULT refer to **the wicked**). You may wish to follow the rendering of a translation in your region that you are familiar with. Alternate translation: \[and the robber curses and disrespects Yahweh] or \[and he blesses the robber whom Yahweh despises]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

In order to follow the original and highlight the parallelism with the previous verse, the ULT leaves out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. Alternate translation: \[He ambushes the afflicted in secret like a lion in cover; he ambushes them to seize them] or \[He waits secretly in ambush like a lion in cover; he waits to ambush and seize the afflicted] or \[He lies in wait in secret like a lion in cover; he lies in wait to seize the afflicted]

## Psalms 10:15 (#5) (id: en_tn_PSA_m5mv)

תִּֽדְרוֹשׁ־רִשְׁע֥⁠וֹ בַל־תִּמְצָֽא

**"May it seek his wickedness, {but} not find {it"**

There is significant debate about who or what may **seek** and **find**. The interpretation suggested here is that the wicked and evil people’s arm (power for harm) is personified as looking to do the evil they have planned but is unable to because Yahweh has broken the arm (power). If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[May the wicked, evil person try to use his power for harm but discover you have destroyed it]; or another common interpretation is that Yahweh will seek out (hunt down, punish) the wicked, evil person’s wickedness until he can no longer find it (because it is eradicated). Alternate translation: \[Hunt down his wickedness until no more can be found]. You may wish to follow the interpretation of a translation commonly used in your region. For more information, see the Psalms layer by layer exegetical discussion at https://psalms.cdbr.org/w/The\_Division\_of\_Psalm\_10:15\.

See: Personification

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 10:15
* **Associated Articles:** Personification (ID: `33302@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms - Chapter 11 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_zn9r)

Psalm 11 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 11 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” (See the Introduction to Psalms.) He will judge the wicked and reward the righteous. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]] and \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

1. David asserts his trust in God (1a)
2. The words of David’s advisors (1b–3\)
3. David’s response to the words of his advisors (4–5\)
4. David asks God to judge righteously (6–7\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Justice

David says that wicked people try to destroy righteous people, but God knows everything that evil people try to do. David says that “Yahweh is righteous” (7\) and “he hates those who love to do violence” (5\). David asks God to judge the wicked (6\) and says that “the upright” will be rewarded by seeing his face (7\). (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 11:0

## Psalms 11:4 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_splx)

יְהוָ֤ה ׀ בְּֽ⁠הֵ֘יכַ֤ל קָדְשׁ֗⁠וֹ יְהוָה֮ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֪יִם כִּ֫סְא֥⁠וֹ

**"Yahweh {is} in his holy temple; Yahweh {is} in the heavens, his throne"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation, if possible. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh is in his holy temple; yes, Yahweh is in the heavens, his throne] or \[Yahweh is in his holy temple; indeed, Yahweh is in the heavens, his throne]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 11:4
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); Throne (ID: `realia:Throne`)

## Psalms 11:4 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_d23s)

יְהוָה֮ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֪יִם כִּ֫סְא֥⁠וֹ

**"Yahweh {is} in the heavens, his throne"**

The psalmist is not distinguishing this **throne** from another throne that is not in heaven. The psalmist is showing God’s greatness compared to human rulers who rule from a throne on earth, by adding that **the heavens** are the place of God’s **throne** (where he rules from). Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh is in the heavens, they are his throne] or \[Yahweh’s throne is in the heavens]

See: Distinguishing Versus Informing or Reminding

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 11:4

## Psalms - Chapter 12 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_c38b)

Psalm 12 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 12 has different types of themes in it. It has elements in it that belong to “lament psalms,” “psalms of trust,” and “imprecatory psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about these types of psalms.

1. David laments that godly people seem to be no more (1\)
2. The deceptive speech of wicked people (2\)
3. David asks Yahweh to stop men who use their speech for evil purposes (3–4\)
4. Yahweh’s response to the mistreatment of “the poor” and “the needy” (5\)
5. Yahweh’s speech is perfect and trustworthy (6\)
6. Yahweh’s “the poor” and “the needy” (7\)
7. David observes the prideful boldness of wicked men as a result of society not condemning their evil actions (8\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh saves “the poor” and “the needy” from the oppressive acts of wicked people

Even though wicked people are temporarily succeeding in oppressing poor and needy people, Yahweh sees and will help “the poor” and “the needy” people who long for deliverance from their oppression (5\). (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

### Words

A major focus of this psalm is the deceptive and prideful words that wicked people use (2–4\). This psalm then shows that Yahweh’s speech, in contrast to the speech of wicked people, is morally perfect and trustworthy (6\).

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 12:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 12:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_nl0l)

אַתָּֽה־יְהוָ֥ה תִּשְׁמְרֵ֑⁠ם

**"You Yahweh, you will keep them"**

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will keep them** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is Yahweh himself who will **keep** and **protect** “the poor” and “the needy” mentioned in verse 5\. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: \[Indeed, it is you Yahweh who will keep them]

**"You Yahweh, you will keep them. You will protect him"**

## Psalms - Chapter 13 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_nza7)

Psalm 13 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 13 is considered to be one of the “lament psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the lament psalms.

1. David calls out to Yahweh regarding Yahweh’s seeming inattention to his troubles (1–2\)
2. David asks Yahweh to “consider” and “answer” him and tells Yahweh what the result will be if Yahweh does not help him (3–4\)
3. David expresses his trust in Yahweh’s “covenant faithfulness” and the fact that he will “rejoice” because of his hope that Yahweh will save him (5\)
4. David will sing to Yahweh because of Yahweh’s kind actions towards him (6\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s help

In this psalm David expresses to Yahweh that he desperately needs his help or else he will die (3\) resulting in his enemies rejoicing at his downfall (4\). David then affirms that he trusts that Yahweh’s “covenant faithfulness” will cause Yahweh to save him from his enemies and he will “sing to Yahweh” and “rejoice” as a result of Yahweh saving him. The word “salvation” in 13:5 refers to help or deliverance from one’s enemies. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]], \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]] and \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/call\-tosummon]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 13:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 13:6 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_c10t)

אָשִׁ֥ירָה לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה כִּ֖י גָמַ֣ל עָלָֽ⁠י

**"I will sing to Yahweh, because he has dealt bountifully with me"**

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: \[Because Yahweh has dealt bountifully with me, I will sing to him]

See: Connect — Reason\-and\-Result Relationship

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 13:6
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship (ID: `33331@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 13:6 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_g998)

גָמַ֣ל עָלָֽ⁠י

**"he has dealt bountifully with me"**

David could be using the past tense **he has dealt bountifully**: (1\) in order to describe something that is going to happen in the future to show that the event will certainly happen. Alternate translation: \[he will deal bountifully with me] or (2\) to refer to things Yahweh has done for him in the past, in which case you can translate this phrase as in the ULT.

See: Irregular Use of Tenses

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 13:6
* **Associated Articles:** Irregular Use of Tenses (ID: `33403@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms - Chapter 14 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_a269)

Psalm 14 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 14 is “wisdom psalm” that describes the difference between how righteous people and wicked people live and the difference between what happens to them. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the Introduction to Psalms.

1. A description of wicked people (1–4\)
2. God punishes wicked people but helps his own people (5–7\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 14:0

## Psalms 14:1 (#5) (id: en_tn_PSA_hlfp)

הִֽשְׁחִ֗יתוּ הִֽתְעִ֥יבוּ עֲלִילָ֗ה

**"They are corrupt, they do a deed abominably"**

These two phrases, **They are corrupt** and **they do a deed abominably**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[They behave in ways that are corrupt and terribly wicked]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms 14:4 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ne4l)

הֲ⁠לֹ֥א יָדְעוּ֮ כָּל־פֹּ֪עֲלֵ֫י אָ֥וֶן אֹכְלֵ֣י עַ֭מִּ⁠י אָ֣כְלוּ לֶ֑חֶם

**"Do they not know, all of the doers of iniquity, the ones eating my people {as} they eat bread"**

The psalmist is using the question form to express amazement that wicked people oppress others without recognizing that God will judge and punish them for doing that. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: \[They ought to know better, the doers of iniquity, the ones eating my people as they eat bread!]

## Psalms 14:7 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_gcqq)

**"Who will give the salvation of Israel from Zion"**

The psalmist is using Mount **Zion**, the location of God’s sanctuary, to represent God himself in the act of providing **salvation** for **Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: \[O that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!] or \[I fervently wish that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!]

## Psalms - Chapter 15 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_j6s2)

Psalm 15 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 15 is considered to be one of the “wisdom psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the wisdom psalms. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wise]])

1. Two parallel rhetorical questions with the same meaning (1\)
2. Ten character traits of the type of person Yahweh lets enter his presence (2–5b)
3. The promised reward for the person meeting Yahweh’s requirements (5c)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### The type of person who may enter into God’s presence

Verse one begins with two questions that are both asking the same thing (parallelism). They are both rhetorical questions that are meant to make the reader think intently about the type of behaviors and attitudes that God requires. Verses 2–5b provide the answer to the questions in verse one. They indicate ten character traits that God requires. The last sentence in verse five is the conclusion to this psalm and states the promised reward for meeting Yahweh’s moral requirements. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/godly]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]] and \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]])

### Moral Conditions for Worship

Scholars have noted that this psalm contains a list of ten different conditions for those who want to participate in worship at the temple. The list consists of three positives in verse two, three negatives in verse three, two positives in verse four, followed by two negatives in verse five. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/temple]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Who do the pronouns “he,” “his,” and “him” refer to?

All occurrences of the pronouns “he,” “his,” and “him” refer to the same type of person. The person being described is not one particular person but rather anyone who exhibits the behaviors described in verses 2–5\.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 15:0


## Psalms 15:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ujjp)

מִי־יָג֣וּר בְּ⁠אָהֳלֶ֑⁠ךָ מִֽי־יִ֝שְׁכֹּ֗ן בְּ⁠הַ֣ר קָדְשֶֽׁ⁠ךָ

**"who may sojourn in your tent? Who may dwell on your holy mountain"**

These two phrases, **who may sojourn in your tent** and **Who may dwell on your holy mountain**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[who may sojourn in your tent, yes, who may dwell on your holy mountain]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 15:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)
