## Psalms - Chapter 16 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_hm6c)

Psalm 16 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 16 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the psalms of trust.

1. David’s prayer (1\)
2. David recalls what he said to Yahweh (2\)
3. David’s delight in godly people (3\)
4. The sorrows of those who pursue gods besides Yahweh and David’s refusal to participate in their idolatry (4\)
5. David acknowledges that Yahweh is in control of his destiny and has greatly blessed him (5–6\)
6. David blesses Yahweh for guiding him (7\)
7. David’s resolve to continually focus on Yahweh (8a)
8. David’s trust that God will protect him from troubles (8b–c)
9. The result of David’s trust in God (9\)
10. David’s trust that God will protect his life (10\)
11. David’s acknowledgement that Yahweh has made him know “the path of life” and that an intimate relationship with Yahweh results in abundant and eternal joys (11\)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “miktam.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Land and inheritance imagery in 16:5–6\.

The historical and cultural background for 16:5–6 is the inheritance of land. 16:6 uses the imagery of measuring cords (lines) which were used to measure and distribute land. These verses probably also have as their background the distribution of the Promised Land to the tribes of Israel and Yahweh promising to be the inheritance of the tribe of Levi. If it would help you to better understand and translate these verses, you can read more about the inheritance of land in Joshua 18–19 and God providing for the Levites in Numbers 18:20–24\.

### Messiah

In Peter’s sermon (Acts 2:14–36\), he quotes Psalm 16:8–11 in 2:25–28 and then explains that David was a prophet and was speaking of the resurrection of the Messiah.
(See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/resurrection]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/anoint]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### What does David mean by “you will not abandon my soul to Sheol. You will not hand over your godly one to see the pit” in 16:10?

The word “Sheol” refers to the place or location of the dead (where dead people go). The word “pit” also refers to the grave. In this verse David is not saying that God will keep him from ever dying. 1 Kings 2:1–10 records that David died of old age. Here David is asserting his trust that God will save him from dying an unnatural death. In other words, he trusts that God will save him from being killed by evil men. Notice that this psalm begins with a prayer for protection. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/hades]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 16:0

Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were actually **the portion of my inheritance**. David is alluding to the inheritance of and distribution of land. (See the Introduction to this psalm for more information.) He means that Yahweh is his most valuable possession and the source of all his blessings and sustenance. בַּל־אֶמּֽוֹט

**"I will not be shaken"**

This is a double negative. David uses the negative particle **not**, with the negative word **shaken** to express a positive meaning strongly. The phrase **I will not be shaken** means that David will remain firm and secure. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: \[he makes me live securely]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of the content of these verses, since 16:8 gives the reason for the result that 16:9 describes. ## Psalms 16:9 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_hoos)

שָׂמַ֣ח לִ֭בִּ⁠י וַ⁠יָּ֣גֶל כְּבוֹדִ֑⁠י

**"my heart is glad, and my glory rejoices"**

These two phrases **my heart is glad** and **my glory rejoices** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[my heart is glad, yes, my whole being rejoices] or \[my heart is glad, yes, my glory rejoices]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 16:9
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Safety (ID: `keyterm:Safety`)

## Psalms 16:10 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_m22q)

לֹא־תַעֲזֹ֣ב נַפְשִׁ֣⁠י לִ⁠שְׁא֑וֹל לֹֽא־תִתֵּ֥ן חֲ֝סִידְ⁠ךָ֗ לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת שָֽׁחַת

**"you will not abandon my soul to Sheol. You will not hand over your faithful one to see the pit"**

These two phrases **you will not abandon my soul to Sheol** and **You will not hand over your godly one to see the pit** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[you will save me, your faithful follower, from death] or \[you will save me, a godly person, from the grave]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 16:10
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Loyal Person (ID: `keyterm:LoyalPerson`); Hell (ID: `place:Hell`)

## Psalms 16:10 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_bdc6)

לֹא־תַעֲזֹ֣ב נַפְשִׁ֣⁠י לִ⁠שְׁא֑וֹל לֹֽא־תִתֵּ֥ן חֲ֝סִידְ⁠ךָ֗ לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת שָֽׁחַת

**"you will not abandon my soul to Sheol. You will not hand over your faithful one to see the pit"**

See the Introduction to this psalm for a discussion of this phrase. Here, David is referring to Yahweh saving him from evil men who might try to kill him. David is not saying that he will not die of old age. Avoid translating this verse in a way that might make it appear that David thinks he will not die of old age.

See: When to Keep Information Implicit

## Psalms - Chapter 17 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_thd2)

Psalm 17 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 17 is one of five psalms that are labeled as “prayers.” (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/innocent]])

1. David asks Yahweh to heed his prayer and pleads his innocence (1–5\)
2. David asserts his belief that God will listen to him and answer him and will save everyone who seeks refuge in God (6–7\)
3. David asks Yahweh to protect him (8–9\)
4. David describes his enemies (10–12\)
5. David asks Yahweh to save him by defeating his enemies who are worldly men (13–14\)
6. David’s hope (15\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 17:0


## Psalms 17:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_djuc)

שִׁמְעָ֤⁠ה יְהוָ֨ה ׀ צֶ֗דֶק הַקְשִׁ֥יבָ⁠ה רִנָּתִ֗⁠י הַאֲזִ֥ינָ⁠ה תְפִלָּתִ֑⁠י

**"Listen, Yahweh {to} righteousness. Pay attention to my cry! Give ear to my prayer"**

These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: \[Please listen, Yahweh, to righteousness. Please pay attention to my cry! Please give ear to my prayer]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 17:1
* **Associated Articles:** Imperatives — Other Uses (ID: `33284@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Deceit (ID: `keyterm:Deceit`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 18 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_enj7)

Psalm 18 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

This is a song by David about Yahweh’s deliverance. This song is also recorded in the Bible in 2 Samuel 22\.

1. David sings to Yahweh that he loves him and calls Yahweh his “strength” (1\)
2. David describes what Yahweh is to him (2\)
3. David recounts that God has answered his prayer and saved him from his enemies when he was in a dangerous situation (3–6\)
4. David compares Yahweh’s act of saving him to three different natural disasters (7–14\)
5. David recounts Yahweh delivering him (15–19\)
6. David gives the reason Yahweh has delivered him (20–27\)
7. David recounts the different things Yahweh has done for him (28–48\)
8. David thanks and praises Yahweh (49\)
9. Yahweh saves David his chosen king and shows covenant faithfulness to David and his descendants forever (50\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Hebrew poetry

The verses of this song by David continually present two phrases that mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases with a word other than “and” in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. But you may find that in some cases it is appropriate to combine the two phrases. For example:

* both phrases

18:23 And I have been blameless with him,
and I have kept myself from my iniquity.
“And I have been blameless with him,
yes, I have kept myself from my iniquity.”

18:21 For I have kept the ways of Yahweh,
and I have not been wicked from my God.
“For I have kept the ways of Yahweh,
no, I have not been wicked from my God.”

* combined into one

18:6 In my distress I called {to} Yahweh,
and to my God I called
“In my distress I called out to Yahweh, my God”

### Extended metaphor

In 7–14, David describes Yahweh coming to help him as being like the greatest natural forces that people of his culture knew, which were an earthquake (7\), a volcano (8\), and a thunderstorm (9–14\). He describes each of these forces in poetic language. In other words, after stating his topic, which is how Yahweh delivered him (6\), David then depicts it with multiple images that communicate multiple ideas. Think about how you might show in your translation that 7–14, while describing three different things, all illustrate the same topic.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Saul (ID: `person:Saul.2`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 18:2 (#6) (id: en_tn_PSA_szq4)

וְ⁠קֶֽרֶן־יִ֝שְׁעִ֗⁠י

**"and the horn of my salvation"**

David is speaking of God’s power to save him as if it were a powerful **horn** of an animal. A horn was a symbol of strength in ancient Israelite culture because animals use their horns as weapons. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[and the one who saves me by his power] or \[and the one who powerfully saves me]

See: Metaphor

## Psalms 18:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_efpc)

וַ⁠תִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַ⁠תִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ וּ⁠מוֹסְדֵ֣י הָרִ֣ים יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַ֝⁠יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ כִּי־חָ֥רָה לֽ⁠וֹ

**"Then the earth shook and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains quaked and shook themselves because it burned to him"**

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: \[Then, because it burned to him, the earth shook and trembled. The foundations of the heavens quaked and shook themselves]

See: Connect — Reason\-and\-Result Relationship

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:7
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship (ID: `33331@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Foundation (ID: `realia:Foundation`)

## Psalms 18:7 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_yej5)

וַ⁠תִּגְעַ֬שׁ \& הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ \& וַ֝⁠יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ

**"Then the earth shook \& and shook themselves"**

The terms that the ULT translates as **shook** and **shook themselves** represent two different verbs in the original. Hebrew had more synonyms for this idea than some other languages may have. David expresses some of these with the verbs translated as **trembled** and **quaked**. It may be necessary for you to use the same words rather than different ones. However, if you do have a variety of terms for this, it would be appropriate to use different words for **shook** and **shook themselves**.

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:7
* **Associated Articles:** Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information (ID: `33273@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Foundation (ID: `realia:Foundation`)

## Psalms 18:7 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_xccy)

וַ⁠תִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַ⁠תִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ

**"Then the earth shook and trembled"**

The terms **shook** and **trembled** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: \[Then the earth shook violently]

See: Doublet

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:7
* **Associated Articles:** Doublet (ID: `33266@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Foundation (ID: `realia:Foundation`)

## Psalms 18:7 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_kk99)

וַ⁠תִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַ⁠תִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ וּ⁠מוֹסְדֵ֣י הָרִ֣ים יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַ֝⁠יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ

**"Then the earth shook and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains quaked and shook themselves"**

David is speaking as if the **earth** and the **foundations of the mountains** were actually a person who could shake and tremble. This expresses how powerfully God responded to David’s prayer. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Then it was as though a violent earthquake occurred and shook the earth and the foundations of the mountains]

* **Associated Articles:** Personification (ID: `33302@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Foundation (ID: `realia:Foundation`)

## Psalms 18:8 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_vnaa)

עָ֘לָ֤ה עָשָׁ֨ן ׀ בְּ⁠אַפּ֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֵשׁ־מִ⁠פִּ֥י⁠ו תֹּאכֵ֑ל גֶּ֝חָלִ֗ים בָּעֲר֥וּ מִמֶּֽ⁠נּוּ

**"Smoke went up from his nose, and fire from his mouth devoured. Coals from him burned"**

David is saying that when Yahweh came to help him, Yahweh’s power was so great that it was like a volcano. David describes the opening at the top of a volcano, from which **Smoke** and **fire** and **Coals** come out, as if it were the **nose** and **mouth** of the volcano. If your readers would be familiar with what a volcano is, you could express in your translation how David is using a volcano as an image to describe Yahweh’s power. If not, you could describe in more general terms how Yahweh’s power is like fire and smoke.

See: Translate Unknowns

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:8
* **Associated Articles:** Translate Unknowns (ID: `33408@UWTranslationManual`)

**"and fire from his mouth devoured"**

David is speaking of the fire that comes from a volcano, which represents God here, as if it were a wild animal that **devoured** its prey. ## Psalms 18:10 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_crav)

וַ⁠יִּרְכַּ֣ב עַל־כְּ֭רוּב וַ⁠יָּעֹ֑ף

## Psalms 18:11 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_b7ew)

יָ֤שֶׁת חֹ֨שֶׁךְ ׀ סִתְר֗⁠וֹ

**"He set darkness his covering"**

David is speaking as if the darkness were actually **set** like a physical object that could be arranged in place. He means that God caused darkness to surround himself. ## Psalms 18:11 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_dwm8)

יָ֤שֶׁת חֹ֨שֶׁךְ ׀ סִתְר֗⁠וֹ סְבִֽיבוֹתָ֥י⁠ו סֻכָּת֑⁠וֹ חֶשְׁכַת־מַ֝֗יִם

**"He set darkness his covering, the booth around him {was} a darkness of waters"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[He set darkness as his covering—yes, the shelter around him was dark storm clouds]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:11
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 18:13 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ipyl)

בָּ֝רָ֗ד וְ⁠גַֽחֲלֵי־אֵֽשׁ

**"hailstones and coals of fire"**

Some ancient manuscripts include the words **hailstones and coals of fire**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts do not have these words. It is possible that during the process of copying, they were repeated here from the previous verse. The ancient Greek translation does not have them. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:13
* **Associated Articles:** Textual Variants (ID: `33405@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

**"hailstones and coals of fire"**

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: \[there were hailstones and coals of fire]

## Psalms 18:14 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_zag7)

וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֣ח חִ֭צָּי⁠ו וַ⁠יְפִיצֵ֑⁠ם וּ⁠בְרָקִ֥ים רָ֝ב וַ⁠יְהֻמֵּֽ⁠ם

**"And he sent out his arrows and he scattered them and lightnings in abundance and he panicked them"**

Here David is using an image within an image. Within the image of a thunderstorm that represents Yahweh coming powerfully to help him, David speaks of lightning bolts as if they were **arrows**. You might be able to clarify this by combining the two parts of this verse, which mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: \[And he sent out lightning bolts like arrows and panicked them so that they scattered]

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:14
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 18:20 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_q28o)

יִגְמְלֵ֣⁠נִי יְהוָ֣ה כְּ⁠צִדְקִ֑⁠י כְּ⁠בֹ֥ר יָ֝דַ֗⁠י יָשִׁ֥יב לִֽ⁠י

**"Yahweh has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands he has given back to me"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh has rewarded me according to my righteousness; yes, according to the cleanness of my hands he has given back to me]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:20
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 18:42 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_imt8)

וְֽ⁠אֶשְׁחָקֵ֗⁠ם כְּ⁠עָפָ֥ר עַל־פְּנֵי־ר֑וּחַ

**"And I beat them fine as dust upon the face of the wind"**

Here David is making a comparison between his defeated enemies and **dust upon the face of the wind**. The point of this comparison is that just as dust upon the face of the wind is completely scattered and powerless, so his enemies became completely defeated and scattered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: \[And I beat them so that they scattered completely like dust blown by the wind]

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 18:42
* **Associated Articles:** Simile (ID: `33314@UWTranslationManual`)

**"And I beat them fine as dust upon the face of the wind"**

## Psalms - Chapter 19 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_sn29)

Psalm 19 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 19 is a psalm about how God has revealed himself and glorifies himself through his physical creation, and how he reveals himself through his written revelation which he gave to the Israelites through Moses.

1. The heavens declare God’s glory (1–4b)
2. The sun in the heavens (4c–6\)
3. The greatness and worth of God’s word and its effect (7–9\)
4. The desirableness of God’s word (10\)
5. The benefit of God’s word (11–12a)
6. Closing prayer (12b–14\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Terms for God’s commands and instructions

The psalmist uses many different words to refer to God’s message to us. You could decide to use a different word for each term, but most languages will not have that many, so just use the words that your language has. In verses 7–9 there are six different terms used for things that God commanded and taught his people.

1. “The law of Yahweh” in 19:7a. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lawofmoses]])
2. “The testimony of Yahweh” in 19:7b. Here the word “testimony” has a similar meaning to the word “law” in 19:7a, making the phrases “The law of Yahweh” and “the testimony of Yahweh” complementary. The phrase “the testimony of Yahweh” refers either to God’s entire law as a whole that he gave to the Israelites or more specifically to his law that he gave them through Moses on Mount Sinai.
3. “The precepts of Yahweh” in verse 19:8a. The word that is translated as “precepts” refers to something that is appointed or mandated so the phrase “the precepts of Yahweh” refers to the things that Yahweh mandated.
4. “The commandment of Yahweh” in 19:8b. See the note on this phrase in 19:8\.
5. “The fear of Yahweh” in 19:9a. See the note on this phrase in 19:9\.
6. “The judgments of Yahweh” in 19:9b. The word translated as “judgments” could also be translated as “ordinances” or “decisions” here and refers to decisions or judgments that are made. Here the phrase “the judgments of Yahweh” refers to the judicial instructions that Yahweh gave the Israelites for handling different types of situations involving people.
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 19:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 19:1 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_r2aa)

הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֗יִם מְֽסַפְּרִ֥ים כְּבֽוֹד־אֵ֑ל וּֽ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יָ֝דָ֗י⁠ו מַגִּ֥יד הָ⁠רָקִֽיעַ

**"The heavens are declaring the glory of God, and the sky is proclaiming the work of his hands"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[The heavens are declaring the glory of God, yes, the sky is proclaiming the work of his hands]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 19:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 19:4 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ehjp)

קַוָּ֗⁠ם \& מִלֵּי⁠הֶ֑ם \& בָּ⁠הֶֽם

## Psalms 19:4 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_z80f)

בְּ⁠כָל־הָ⁠אָ֨רֶץ ׀ יָ֘צָ֤א קַוָּ֗⁠ם

**"Their line has gone out through all of the earth"**

The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) and the Peshitta (the Syriac translation of the Bible) read “Their voice” instead of “their line.” That may have been the original reading, particularly since it would then make this line a parallelism with the second line in the verse with “Their voice” and **their words** being parallel ideas. At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have accidentally left out the additional Hebrew letter that would have spelled “Their voice” rather than **Their line**. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See: Textual Variants

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 19:4
* **Associated Articles:** Textual Variants (ID: `33405@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 19:5 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_z5g4)

**"and that is like a bridegroom coming out from his chamber"**

The point of this comparison is that just as **a bridegroom coming out from his chamber** is satisfied, joyful and radiant so is the sun as it rises. (Here the word **chamber** refers to a bedroom.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: \[and that joyfully rises like a bridegroom coming out from his chamber] or \[and it comes out joyfully and eagerly like a bridegroom leaving his bedroom]

## Psalms - Chapter 20 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_h99t)

Psalm 20 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 20 is considered to be one of the “royal psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the royal psalms.

1. Prayer for the king that Yahweh would protect and help him in battle (1–2\)
2. Prayer that Yahweh would accept the king’s offerings (3\)
3. Prayer that Yahweh would fulfill the king’s desires and plans (4\)
4. Anticipation of Yahweh giving his king victory (5\)
5. Expression of confidence in Yahweh (6–8\)
6. Closing prayer (9\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Trust

In verse 7 David asserts that trusting in Yahweh is better than trusting in military might. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### In verses 1–5 who do the pronouns “you” and “your” refer to?

In this psalm all occurrences of the pronouns “you” and “your” that occur in verses 1–5 are singular and refer to Yahweh’s anointed king mentioned in verse 6\. Because verse 6 identifies who the pronouns “you” and “your” refer to, you do not need to make this explicit in your translation. Also, if your language has both singular and plural second person pronouns, you should use the singular forms each time you translate the pronouns “you” and “your” in verses 1–5\.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 20:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 20:0 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_qhb5)

## Psalms 20:2 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_gxv3)

יִשְׁלַֽח־עֶזְרְ⁠ךָ֥ מִ⁠קֹּ֑דֶשׁ וּ֝⁠מִ⁠צִּיּ֗וֹן יִסְעָדֶֽ⁠ךָּ

**"May he send you help from the sanctuary and support you from Zion"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[May he send you help from the sanctuary, yes, may he support you from Zion]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 20:2
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Jerusalem (ID: `place:Jerusalem`)

## Psalms - Chapter 21 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_mq8x)

Psalm 21 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 21 is considered to be one of the “royal psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the royal psalms.

1. The king rejoices in Yahweh’s strength (1\)
2. Yahweh’s blessing of his chosen king (2–6\)
3. The king’s trust in Yahweh (7\)
4. The king will defeat his enemies with Yahweh’s help (8–12\)
5. Final words regarding Yahweh’s strength and power (13\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Pronouns

There is a shift in how Yahweh is referred to in this psalm. In verses 1–6 David uses second person pronouns when Yahweh is addressed. In verse 7 Yahweh is referred to in the third person as “Yahweh” and as “the Most High.” In verses 8–13 David shifts back to using second person pronouns when Yahweh is being addressed. (See: First, Second or Third Person)

In this psalm, when the pronouns “you,” “we,” “them,” “their,” and “they” are used, it may at times be unclear to whom these pronouns are referring to. For help translating these pronouns, see the notes in the individual verses where these pronouns occur. (See: Pronouns — When to Use Them)

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 21:0
* **Associated Articles:** First, Second or Third Person (ID: `33256@UWTranslationManual`); Pronouns — When to Use Them (ID: `33424@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 21:8 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_kxnm)

תִּמְצָ֣א יָ֭דְ⁠ךָ לְ⁠כָל־אֹיְבֶ֑י⁠ךָ יְ֝מִֽינְ⁠ךָ תִּמְצָ֥א שֹׂנְאֶֽי⁠ךָ

**"Your hand will find all of your enemies; your right hand will find the ones hating you"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Your hand will find all of your enemies, indeed, your right hand will find those who hate you]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 21:8
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

**"Your hand"**

**"Your hand will find \& your right hand will find"**

David is using **Your hand will find** as a common expression of his culture to mean “You will reach” or “You will overtake.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[You will reach … you will overtake]

## Psalms - Chapter 22 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_y7hl)

Psalm 22 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 22 contains several different but related themes of lament, prayer, trust, and hope for the future. Verses 1–21 are a lament. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about psalms of lament. Verses 22–31 praise Yahweh for his deliverance and kingship over the nations, and the worship he will receive in the future. Many Bible scholars consider Psalm 22 to be one of the “messianic psalms” because different New Testament authors quote parts of this psalm in relation to Jesus and because Jesus quotes the first line of verse 1 while on the cross. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the messianic psalms. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/crucify]] and \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]])

1. An anguished call to God (1–2\)
2. An affirmation of God’s holiness and past deliverance of the Israelites (3–5\)
3. David describes his situation (6–18\)
4. A prayer for help (19–21\)
5. Yahweh’s deliverance of David results in Yahweh being praised (22–26\)
6. People from all parts of the world, all people groups, and rich and poor people will turn to Yahweh and worship him as king (27–29\)
7. Future generations will praise Yahweh and will be told about his saving acts (30–31\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 22:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`); Deer (ID: `fauna:Deer`)

## Psalms 22:16 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_q41h)

כָּ֝⁠אֲרִ֗י

**"like the lion"**

The Hebrew text that the ULT is translated from reads **like the lion**. Other ancient manuscripts have a verb (instead of the noun translated as **like the lion**). At one point in the process of transmission, scribes may have mistakenly changed the last letter of the verb with the meaning “they have pierced” to a different (and similar looking) letter, resulting in the word **like the lion**. All the ancient versions of the Old Testament, as well as the early Jewish sources have verb forms instead of the noun form **like the lion**. The original text probably had the verb meaning “they have pierced” instead of the noun form translated **like the lion**. For this reason, you may wish to use the verb “they have pierced.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use whatever form it uses.

See: Textual Variants

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 22:16
* **Associated Articles:** Textual Variants (ID: `33405@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Dog (ID: `fauna:Dog`); Lion (ID: `fauna:Lion`)

## Psalms 22:29 (#7) (id: en_tn_PSA_facn)

**"all of the ones going down to the dust, even his self he kept not alive"**

These two phrases **all of the ones going down to the dust** and **even his self he kept not alive** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[all of the ones going down to the dust, that is, those who cannot keep themselves alive]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms - Chapter 23 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_r1f6)

Psalm 23 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 23 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the “psalms of trust.”

1. Yahweh depicted as a good and trustworthy shepherd (1–4\)
2. Yahweh depicted as a good and generous banquet host (5\)
3. David affirms his trust in Yahweh’s faithful goodness and love and asserts that he will dwell with him forever (6\)

Translation Issues in this Psalm
--------------------------------

### Metaphor

Psalm 23:1–4 is an extended metaphor in which David speaks of Yahweh as if he were a shepherd, and of himself as a sheep. Psalm 23:5 is a metaphor in which David depicts himself as a guest at a banquet at which Yahweh is the host. (See: Biblical Imagery — Extended Metaphors and Metaphor)

### Referring to Yahweh in the first person and second person

In verses 1–3 and 6, David writes about Yahweh in the second person. In verses 4–5, David addresses Yahweh directly, in the first person. Yahweh’s name is used in verses 1 and 6, but in verses 2–5 pronouns are used. Second person pronouns are used in verses 2–3 when referring to Yahweh, and David addresses God directly in verses 4–5 and therefore uses first person pronouns. If your language uses pronouns, use the appropriate pronouns in verses 2–5\. (See: First, Second or Third Person)

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 23:0
* **Associated Articles:** Biblical Imagery — Extended Metaphors (ID: `33272@UWTranslationManual`); Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`); First, Second or Third Person (ID: `33256@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms - Chapter 24 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_cw5j)

Psalm 24 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 24 is a “royal psalm.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the royal psalms. It is also a psalm that the Israelites used for their processional liturgy as they entered Jerusalem or as they proceeded to Yahweh’s Tabernacle on Mount Zion in Jerusalem. In this psalm there is a clear call\-and\-response pattern in which someone leading the procession would have called out parts of this psalm (verse 3, 8a, 10a), and those in the procession would have responded and answered with the words in verses 4–6, 8b, and 10b–c.

Among Bible scholars there are different opinions about the exact setting and context of this psalm. Because this psalm begins with “of David” the events in this psalm are most likely during David’s lifetime.

1. Yahweh created the world and it belongs to him (1–2\)
2. Yahweh requires righteousness to enter his presence and rewards and vindicates those who are righteous (3–6\)
3. Yahweh is the glorious and victorious king (7–10\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Righteous people

“Clean hands” and a “pure heart” (being morally pure in action and in thought and intention) are required to enter Yahweh’s presence. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Rhetorical Questions

David uses three rhetorical questions in this psalm. Each rhetorical question forms a unit with a response. The three rhetorical questions are found in verses 3, 8, and 10\. (See: Rhetorical Question)

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 24:0
* **Associated Articles:** Rhetorical Question (ID: `33310@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 24:2 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_a94o)

כִּי

**"For"**

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: \[This is because]

See: Connect — Reason\-and\-Result Relationship

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 24:2
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship (ID: `33331@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 24:2 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_g1vd)

**"For he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers"**

By **the seas** and **the rivers** David means the waters that existed before God created the dry land. David, and people in his culture, thought of the world as being founded and placed by God upon subterannean waters. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: \[For he has founded it upon the waters that were there before creation] or \[For he has founded it upon the deep waters under the earth]

## Psalms 24:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_kxov)

**"Who may ascend on the mountain of Yahweh? And who may stand in his holy place"**

David is using questions to cause his readers to think deeply about who is qualified to approach God. David is not asking for information, but is emphasizing that only people who meet certain requirements can approach God. If you would not use rhetorical questions for this purpose in your language, you could translate his questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: \[Only certain people may ascend on the mountain of Yahweh! Only certain people may stand in his holy place!]

## Psalms - Chapter 25 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_utp4)

Psalm 25 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 25 has several different themes or topics within it. These include assertions of trust in Yahweh, lament (complaints about the present situation), and asking Yahweh for forgiveness of sin, deliverance from enemies and troubles, and for guidance. This psalm is an acrostic poem which follows the order of the Hebrew alphabet, with a few exceptions.

1. David’s first prayer (1–7\)
2. Yahweh guides humble people in the right way to live (8–9\)
3. Yahweh’s positive response to “the ones keeping his covenant and his testimonies” (10\)
4. David’s second prayer (11\)
5. Ways that Yahweh blesses those who fear him (12–14\)
6. David looks to Yahweh for deliverance from his enemies (15\)
7. David’s third prayer (16–22\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s guidance of David described using the metaphor of “path” and a “way”

In verses 4–5, 8–9, and 12 David describes the right way to live, the way that Yahweh desires a person to live, as a “path” and a “way.” David asks Yahweh to lead him in this proper way of living (4–5\), says that Yahweh will teach humble people his “way” (8–9\), and will teach those who fear him the proper “way” (12\). See the individual notes in these verses for specific translation guidance. (Because David uses a parallelism in verse 4, we know that the words “ways/way” and “paths” have the same meaning in these particular verses.)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Singular forms of “you” and “your.”

In verses 1–7, 11, and 16–22 David prays directly to Yahweh. Each time David uses the pronouns “you” and “your” in these verses they are the singular form (in the language he wrote in, Hebrew) because they refer to Yahweh. If your language has singular and plural forms of the pronouns “you” and “your,” make sure you use the singular forms in these verses. (See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular)

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 25:0
* **Associated Articles:** Forms of ‘You’ — Singular (ID: `33321@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 25:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ig8h)

נַפְשִׁ֥⁠י אֶשָּֽׂא

**"I lift up my soul"**

David is speaking of his earnest prayer and worship as if he were to physically **lift up** his **soul** to Yahweh. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[I pour out my heart] or \[I come in prayer]

**"do not let me have shame; do not let my enemies exult over me"**

If the imperative forms do not communicate polite requests in your language, you could use forms that communicate polite requests. ## Psalms - Chapter 26 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_q9dz)

Psalm 26 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

1. David asks Yahweh to give him justice because of his righteous lifestyle (1–6a)
2. David vows to thank Yahweh and recount all his wondrous deeds (6b–7\)
3. David proclaims that he loves to be in Yahweh’s presence in the Tabernacle (8\)
4. David asks Yahweh not to punish him with the wicked (9–10\)
5. David vows to live with integrity and asks Yahweh to redeem him and be gracious to him as a result (11\)
6. David’s closing words (12\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Praise

The psalmist delights in praising God and doing good deeds. It is striking how this psalm uses the first person pronoun. This is an individual psalm of petition. Each of the four petitions are accompanied with various claims. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 26:0

בְּחָנֵ֣⁠נִי יְהוָ֣ה וְ⁠נַסֵּ֑⁠נִי

**"Examine me, Yahweh, and test me"**

These two phrases, **Examine me** and **test me**, mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh, examine and test me]

## Psalms - Chapter 27 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_ru1e)

Psalm 27 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 27 is considered to be one of the “psalms of trust.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the psalms of trust.

1. David declares his confidence in God (1–6\)
2. David prays for help (7–12\)
3. David affirms his faith in God and calls on others to patiently endure (13–14\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s help

Because of God’s help, he has nothing to fear, no matter what happens. The psalmist shows his confidence in God; he also asks God for help.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 27:0


## Psalms 27:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_u8bv)

יְהוָ֤ה ׀ אוֹרִ֣⁠י

**"Yahweh is my light"**

David is speaking of **Yahweh** as if he were **light** that illuminates, guides, helps, and encourages him. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh is like light to me]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 27:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Salvation (ID: `keyterm:Salvation`); David (ID: `person:David`); Fear (ID: `keyterm:Fear`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); Fortress (ID: `realia:Fortress`)

David is using two rhetorical questions, **whom will I fear** and **whom will I dread**, to emphasize that he does not fear anyone because Yahweh protects him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements. ## Psalms 27:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_l0wj)

אִם־תַּחֲנֶ֬ה עָלַ֨⁠י ׀ מַחֲנֶה֮ לֹֽא־יִירָ֪א לִ֫בִּ֥⁠י אִם־תָּק֣וּם עָ֭לַ⁠י מִלְחָמָ֑ה בְּ֝⁠זֹ֗את אֲנִ֣י בוֹטֵֽחַ

**"Though an army encamps against me, my heart will not fear; though war arises against me, in this I will be confident"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Though an army encamps against me and war arises against me, my heart will not fear but will be confident]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 27:3
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Trust (ID: `keyterm:LeanOn`); Fear (ID: `keyterm:Fear`)

## Psalms 27:4 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_v17t)

אַחַ֤ת ׀ שָׁאַ֣לְתִּי מֵֽ⁠אֵת־יְהוָה֮ אוֹתָ֪⁠הּ אֲבַ֫קֵּ֥שׁ

**"One {thing} I have asked from Yahweh, that I will seek"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[One thing I have asked from Yahweh, yes, this is what I will seek]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 27:4
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); House (ID: `realia:House`)

## Psalms - Chapter 28 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_a18t)

Psalm 28 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 28 begins as a lament psalm and then transitions into praise, thanksgiving, and affirmation of his trust in Yahweh.

1. David prays for deliverance (1–2\)
2. David asks God to judge the wicked (3–5\)
3. David praises God and affirms his goodness (6–9\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Trust

David trusted God completely and God rescued him. This is similar to Psalm 7 and 17 because it is an individual psalm of lament. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Text variant in 28:8

In 28:8 some Hebrew manuscripts contain the Hebrew word that could be literally translated as “for them” while other Hebrew manuscripts contain the word that could be literally translated as “for his people.” The Hebrew manuscript that the ULT follows contains the word that reads “for them” but the ULT translates this word as “for his people” because this word is being considered an alternate spelling of the word “for his people.” For the reasoning behind this decision, see the portion on “The Text of v. 8a” in this video produced by the “Psalms: Layer by Layer” project titled “Psalm 28: Exegetical Issues.” See the video at (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v\=QHlm\_UCsX\-A\&t\=1037s)

“The Psalms: Layer by Layer” videos are part of the “Psalms: Layer by Layer” project, which is run by Scriptura (formerly Cambridge Digital Bible Research).

To visit the Psalms: Layer by Layer website go to https://psalms.scriptura.org. These videos are used under CC BY

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 28:0

If the imperative form would not communicate a polite request in your language, you could use a different form that would communicate a polite request. \[Please give them … please give to them … please return to them] or \[I ask that you give them … I ask that you give to them … I ask that you return to them]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 28:4
* **Associated Articles:** Imperatives — Other Uses (ID: `33284@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 28:4 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_bdpx)

תֶּן־לָ⁠הֶ֣ם כְּ⁠פָעֳלָ⁠ם֮ וּ⁠כְ⁠רֹ֪עַ מַֽעַלְלֵ֫י⁠הֶ֥ם כְּ⁠מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה יְ֭דֵי⁠הֶם תֵּ֣ן לָ⁠הֶ֑ם

**"Give to them according to their work and according to the evil of their deeds; give to them according to the work of their hands"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Give to them according to their work, yes, according to the evil of their deeds and the work of their hands]

## Psalms - Chapter 29 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_b4tt)

Psalm 29 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 29 is a “psalm of praise.” It tells how Yahweh rules all nature.

1. A call to worship (1–2\)
2. Declarations of God’s voice over creation depict natural phenomena (3–9\)
3. The Lord sovereignty (10–11\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### The Cultural and Religious Background of verses 3–10

The cultural and religious background of verses 3–10 is the worship of the false gods of the nations who lived around the Israelites. Verses 3–10 are a firm declaration of Yahweh’s power and rule over the entire universe and an implicit denunciation of putting trust in false gods such as the Canaanite god Baal.

Because David does not state the historical and religious background information explicitly in verses 3–10, it is recommended that you not include this information either but if you are using footnotes or chapter introductions in your translation, you may wish to include some of the background information there if it would help your readers.

### Yahweh’s power

God is powerful. All he has to do is to speak in order to control nature.

For an overview of Psalm 29 and help understanding some of the important exegetical and poetical issues in this psalm, see the Psalms: Layer by Layer videos below. These videos are part of the Psalms: Layer by Layer project, which is run by Scriptura (formerly Cambridge Digital Bible Research).
See their overview video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v\=\_aoWN\_yFa0E) and top three exegetical issues in Psalm 29 video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v\=nnL109G57mg\&t\=452s) and their top three poetic features of Psalm 29 video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v\=ygoKm9HWKQU\&t\=181s) on YouTube.

To visit the Psalms: Layer by Layer website go to https://psalms.scriptura.org. These videos are used under CC BY

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 29:0

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. **"And he makes Lebanon skip like a calf and Sirion like a son of wild oxen"**

## Psalms - Chapter 30 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_eee3)

Psalm 30 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 30 is a psalm of praise and thanksgiving to God. The psalmist was so sick that he was near death, but God healed him.

1. Call to praise and testimony (1–5\)
2. The crisis remembered (6–7\)
3. The prayer for help (8–10\)
4. The deliverance and vow of praise (11–12\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### The possibility of David dying from sickness

In this psalm David recounts how he was close to death and then pleaded with God. David asked God to heal him and told God that if he died, it would not benefit God, since dead people do not praise God in this life. God healed David with the result that David sings praises to God and thanks him.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 30:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Offering (ID: `keyterm:Offering`); Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`); House (ID: `realia:House`)

## Psalms 30:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_pq51)

אֲרוֹמִמְ⁠ךָ֣ יְ֭הוָה כִּ֣י דִלִּיתָ֑⁠נִי וְ⁠לֹא־שִׂמַּ֖חְתָּ אֹיְבַ֣⁠י לִֽ⁠י

**"I will extol you, Yahweh, for you have drawn me up and have not let the ones being hostile to me rejoice over me"**

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: \[Because you have drawn me up and have not let the ones being hostile to me rejoice over me, I will extol you, Yahweh] or \[Yahweh, because you have drawn me up and have not let the ones being hostile to me rejoice over me, I will extol you]

See: Connect — Reason\-and\-Result Relationship

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 30:1
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Reason-and-Result Relationship (ID: `33331@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 30:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_cf5g)

הֶֽעֱלִ֣יתָ מִן־שְׁא֣וֹל נַפְשִׁ֑⁠י חִ֝יִּיתַ֗⁠נִי מ⁠יורדי־בֽוֹר

**"you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you have kept me alive from the ones going down to the pit"**

The word **Sheol** refers to the place of the dead, where dead people go, and the word **pit** also refers to the grave. These two phrases, **you have brought up my soul from Sheol** and **you have kept me alive from the ones going down to the pit**, mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[you have brought up my soul from Sheol, yes, you have kept me alive from the ones going down to the pit]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 30:3
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Hell (ID: `place:Hell`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 31 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_j2an)

Psalm 31 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 31 is considered to be one of the “psalms of deliverance.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the psalms of deliverance.

1. Declaration of trust (1–8\)
2. Lament over suffering (9–13\)
3. Affirmation of faith (14–18\)
4. Praise and thanksgiving (19–22\)
5. Final Exhortation (23–24\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Abandonment

Even though everyone deserted and despised the psalmist, God did not abandon him.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 31:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 31:0 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_h2ro)

לַ⁠מְנַצֵּ֗חַ

## Psalms 31:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_wyqo)

בְּ⁠ךָ֖ יְהוָ֣ה חָ֭סִיתִי

**"In you, Yahweh, I take refuge"**

Here David is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a physical place of safety or shelter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[I trust in you, Yahweh, to keep me safe] or \[I depend on you, Yahweh, to protect me]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 31:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Seek Refugue (ID: `keyterm:SeekfindRefuge`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 31:1 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_p1th)

אַל־אֵב֣וֹשָׁה לְ⁠עוֹלָ֑ם בְּ⁠צִדְקָתְ⁠ךָ֥ פַלְּטֵֽ⁠נִי

**"do not ever let me have shame; in your righteousness deliver me"**

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: \[please do not ever let me have shame; please deliver me in your righteousness]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 31:1
* **Associated Articles:** Imperatives — Other Uses (ID: `33284@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Seek Refugue (ID: `keyterm:SeekfindRefuge`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 31:2 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_su51)

הֱיֵ֤ה לִ֨⁠י ׀ לְֽ⁠צוּר־מָ֭עוֹז לְ⁠בֵ֥ית מְצוּד֗וֹת

* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 31:2 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_tqss)

**"be for me a rocky summit of refuge, a dwelling place of strongholds"**

David is using these possessive forms, **a rocky summit of refuge** and **a dwelling place of strongholds**, to describe places that are characterized by providing refuge and strength. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive forms for this, you could express these ideas in another way. Alternate translation: \[be for me a rocky summit that provides refuge, a stronghold in which to dwell]

## Psalms 31:3 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_ki3f)

תַּֽנְחֵ֥⁠נִי וּֽ⁠תְנַהֲלֵֽ⁠נִי

## Psalms 31:3 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_ueon)

תַּֽנְחֵ֥⁠נִי וּֽ⁠תְנַהֲלֵֽ⁠נִי

**"you lead me and guide me"**

Here the Hebrew verbs that the ULT translates as **you lead me and guide me** could be: (1\) expressing a general truth that has been part of David’s ongoing experience. If you decide this is the meaning, then you can translate the two verbs in this phrase in a similar way to the ULT. (2\) expressing something that will happen in the future. Alternate translation: \[you will lead me and guide me] or (3\) a request that is a prayer to Yahweh. (This option is less likely since David does not use the imperative forms of these verbs as would be expected if these verbs were meant to be requests.) Alternate translation: \[lead me and guide me] or \[please lead me and guide me]

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 31:3

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Fortress (ID: `realia:Fortress`)

**"you lead me and guide me"**

## Psalms 31:10 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_kmf0)

כִּ֤י כָל֪וּ בְ⁠יָג֡וֹן חַיַּ⁠י֮ וּ⁠שְׁנוֹתַ֪⁠י בַּ⁠אֲנָ֫חָ֥ה כָּשַׁ֣ל בַּ⁠עֲוֺנִ֣⁠י כֹחִ֑⁠י וַ⁠עֲצָמַ֥⁠י עָשֵֽׁשׁוּ

**"For my life has come to an end with sorrow, and my years with groaning; my strength fails from my iniquity, and my bones waste away"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[For my life comes to an end with sorrow, yes, my years with groaning; my strength fails from my iniquity, indeed, my bones waste away]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 31:10
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Strength (ID: `keyterm:Strength`); Passion (ID: `keyterm:Ardour`)

## Psalms 31:10 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_ghjv)

כִּ֤י כָל֪וּ בְ⁠יָג֡וֹן חַיַּ⁠י֮

**"For my life has come to an end with sorrow"**

By **For my life has come to an end with sorrow**, David means that his life is being consumed or shortened by grief and distress. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: \[For my life is being consumed by sorrow] or \[For sorrow is shortening my life]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

## Psalms 31:20 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_pkz7)

תַּסְתִּירֵ֤⁠ם ׀ בְּ⁠סֵ֥תֶר פָּנֶי⁠ךָ֮ מֵֽ⁠רֻכְסֵ֫י אִ֥ישׁ תִּצְפְּנֵ֥⁠ם בְּ⁠סֻכָּ֗ה מֵ⁠רִ֥יב לְשֹׁנֽוֹת

**"You hide them in the hiding\-place of your presence from the plots of man; you hide them in a shelter from the strife of tongues"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[You hide them in the safety of your presence, protecting them from those who plot against them and from cruel words]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 31:20
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

**"You hide them in the hiding\-place of your presence from the plots of man"**

Here David is speaking of **the hiding\-place of your presence** as if it were a physical shelter where Yahweh could hide people from danger. David means that Yahweh protects people by his divine presence and power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[You protect them by your presence from the plots of man]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 31:20
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms - Chapter 32 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_le2f)

Psalm 32 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 32 is a psalm about confession of sin. It is considered to be one of the “penitential” psalms. See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the penitential psalms. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/confess]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]])

1. The type of person who God says is blessed (1–2\)
2. The results of concealing one’s sin (3–4\)
3. David confesses his sin to Yahweh and Yahweh forgives his sin (5\)
4. David gives reasons for confessing one’s sin to Yahweh (6–7\)
5. David instructs his readers (8–9\)
6. Conclusion (10–11\)

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a “maskil.” See the discussion of that term in the introduction to Psalms.

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Confession of sin

This Psalm tells of the sorrow of unconfessed sin. It also tells of the blessing of confession and of receiving God’s forgiveness. It is a blessing when God forgives sin. Trouble comes when sin is hidden and not confessed. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/forgive]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Who is speaking in verses 8–9?

Among Bible scholars there are several different views regarding who is speaking in verses 8 and 9\. Some Bible scholars think that it is David speaking, and others think that it is God speaking. Because these verses do not explicitly state who is speaking, you should not indicate who the speaker is in your translation.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 32:0

## Psalms 32:1 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_ymli)

נְֽשׂוּי־פֶּ֗שַׁע כְּס֣וּי חֲטָאָֽה

**"the one whose transgression is lifted up, the one covered from sin"**

These two phrases **the one whose transgression is lifted up** and **the one covered from sin** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be helpful in your language to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[the one whose transgression is lifted up, that is, whose sin is covered]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 32:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 32:5 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_u4lz)

חַטָּאתִ֨⁠י אוֹדִ֪יעֲ⁠ךָ֡ וַ⁠עֲוֺ֘נִ֤⁠י לֹֽא־כִסִּ֗יתִי

**"My sin I acknowledged to you, and my guilt I did not cover"**

These two phrases **My sin I acknowledged to you** and **my guilt I did not cover** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[I confessed my sin to you—I did not hide my guilt]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms - Chapter 33 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_m4ih)

Psalm 33 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 33 is a “psalm of praise” telling how great God is.

1. Call the righteous to praise Yahweh (1–3\)
2. Yahweh’s word and works are true and powerful (4–9\)
3. Yahweh rules over nations and cares for his people (10–19\)
4. Trust and hope in Yahweh’s steadfast love (20–22\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s power

Yahweh is the creator and also the God of his people, Israel. Whatever he plans works out. He alone provides safety in battle.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 33:0

This is an imperative, but it communicates an exhortation rather than a command. The psalmist is encouraging **righteous ones** to worship. If the imperative does not communicate an exhortation for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates an exhortation or invitation. ## Psalms 33:6 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_wxxa)

בִּ⁠דְבַ֣ר יְ֭הוָה שָׁמַ֣יִם נַעֲשׂ֑וּ וּ⁠בְ⁠ר֥וּחַ פִּ֝֗י⁠ו כָּל־צְבָאָֽ⁠ם

**"By the word of Yahweh, the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth, all of their host"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[By the word of Yahweh the heavens were made, indeed, by the breath of his mouth, all of their host] or \[By his command, Yahweh made the heavens and everything in them]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 33:6
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); Word of the Lord (ID: `keyterm:WordOfTheLord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 34 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_az5s)

Psalm 34 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 34 is a “psalm of thanksgiving.” It teaches that living right leads to a good life.

1. Praise Yahweh and testify of his deliverance (1–7\)
2. Invite others to trust and fear Yahweh (8–14\)
3. Yahweh watches over and rescues the righteous (15–22\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s help

Good people can have problems, but God brings them through these. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 34:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Achish (ID: `person:Achish`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 35 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_d3ln)

Psalm 35 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

This psalm is considered to be one of the “imprecatory psalms.” See the Introduction to Psalms for more information about the imprecatory psalms.

1. Ask Yahweh to fight against adversaries (1–10\)
2. Lament unjust hatred and false accusations (11–18\)
3. Pray for vindication and justice from Yahweh (19–28\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Enemies

When David’s enemies were sick, he tried to comfort them, but when he was in trouble his enemies used this as a time to attack him.

Translation Issues in this Psalm
--------------------------------

### Imperatives

Throughout this psalm, David is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative form which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language to address a superior in this way, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 35:0


## Psalms 35:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_zyqh)

רִיבָ֣⁠ה יְ֭הוָה אֶת־יְרִיבַ֑⁠י לְ֝חַ֗ם אֶת־לֹֽחֲמָֽ⁠י

**"Yahweh, oppose my opponents; fight those fighting me"**

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[contend against those who fight against me]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 35:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 35:1 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_wvp9)

**"Yahweh, oppose my opponents; fight those fighting me"**

The words **oppose** and **fight** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. Here and throughout the psalm where this form is used, it may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh, please oppose my opponents; please fight those fighting me]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

## Psalms 35:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_syho)

**"For without cause they hid for me a pit, their net; without cause they dug for my life"**

The phrases **they hid for me a pit, their net; without cause they dug for my life** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have accidentally switched the order of the words for “pit” and “their net.” Many translations put “their net” first so that “a pit” begins the second line, and you may want to do the same. **"Let destruction overtake him; he does not know. Let the net that he hid catch him. In destruction, let him fall into it"**

Throughout this verse, the pronouns **him** and **he** are singular, but they refer to all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms as modeled in the UST.

See: Collective Nouns

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 35:8
* **Associated Articles:** Collective Nouns (ID: `33324@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Casting Net (ID: `realia:CastingNet`); Net (ID: `realia:Net`)

## Psalms 35:8 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_jspp)

תְּבוֹאֵ֣⁠הוּ שׁוֹאָה֮ לֹֽא־יֵ֫דָ֥ע

**"Let destruction overtake him; he does not know"**

David is speaking of **destruction** as if it were a living thing that could a dangerous animal that would chase the enemies down and suddenly attack them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Let them be surprised because you destroy them suddenly]

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Casting Net (ID: `realia:CastingNet`); Net (ID: `realia:Net`)

## Psalms 35:8 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_gv8l)

וְ⁠רִשְׁתּ֣⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁר־טָמַ֣ן תִּלְכְּד֑⁠וֹ בְּ֝⁠שׁוֹאָ֗ה יִפָּל־בָּֽ⁠הּ

**"Let the net that he hid catch him. In destruction, let him fall into it"**

David is describing the ironic reversal in which the traps his enemies prepared will instead ensnare them. The **net** they set for David will **catch** them, and they will fall to their own **destruction** into the “pit” they “dug.” If a speaker of your language would not express this reversal in this way, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Let his own trap catch him; let him fall into ruin by his own scheming]

See: Irony

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 35:8
* **Associated Articles:** Irony (ID: `33288@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Casting Net (ID: `realia:CastingNet`); Net (ID: `realia:Net`)

## Psalms 35:9 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ojd8)

וְ֭⁠נַפְשִׁ⁠י תָּגִ֣יל בַּ⁠יהוָ֑ה תָּ֝שִׂישׂ

**"But my soul will be joyful in Yahweh; it will rejoice"**

David is using the term **my soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: \[But I will be joyful in Yahweh; I will rejoice]

## Psalms 35:9 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_djno)

וְ֭⁠נַפְשִׁ⁠י תָּגִ֣יל

**"But my soul will be joyful"**

David uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the destruction of his enemies and his own joy in Yahweh. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: \[Despite all this, my soul will be joyful in Yahweh]

## Psalms 35:9 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_dxfz)

**"will be joyful in Yahweh; it will rejoice"**

The terms **joyful** and **rejoice** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: \[my soul will celebrate with great gladness]

## Psalms 35:10 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_oveb)

יְהוָ֗ה מִ֥י כָ֫מ֥וֹ⁠ךָ מַצִּ֣יל עָ֭נִי מֵ⁠חָזָ֣ק מִמֶּ֑⁠נּוּ וְ⁠עָנִ֥י וְ֝⁠אֶבְי֗וֹן מִ⁠גֹּזְלֽ⁠וֹ

**"Yahweh, who is like you, rescuing the oppressed from those stronger than them and the oppressed and needy from those robbing them"**

David is using the question form to emphasize that no one is comparable to Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: \[There is no one like you, Yahweh! You rescue the oppressed from those stronger than them and the oppressed and needy from those robbing them.]

See: Rhetorical Question

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 35:10
* **Associated Articles:** Rhetorical Question (ID: `33310@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 35:14 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_nx97)

כְּ⁠רֵֽעַ־כְּ⁠אָ֣ח לִ֭⁠י הִתְהַלָּ֑כְתִּי כַּ⁠אֲבֶל־אֵ֝֗ם קֹדֵ֥ר שַׁחֽוֹתִי

**"As {for} a friend, as {for} a brother to me, I walked about; as {one} lamenting {for} a mother, mourning, I bowed down"**

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. ## Psalms 35:15 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_hjvu)

נֵ֭כִים וְ⁠לֹ֣א יָדַ֑עְתִּי

**"the stricken {ones}, and I did not know"**

The word translated as **the stricken ones** represents the written Hebrew text. This could refer to the mockers imitating David’s lameness as possibly described in verse 16, if vowels are used to read “deformity” instead of “food” in that verse. However, scholars have proposed that changing one vowel here would make the word “the strikers,” which seems to fit better the meaning of this verse. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: \[the strikers I did not even know]

See: Alternative Readings

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 35:15

## Psalms - Chapter 36 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_a634)

Psalm 36 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 36 is a “psalm of praise.” It speaks of how good God is to those who love him.

1. The depth of human sin (1–4\)
2. The greatness of Yahweh’s steadfast love (5–9\)
3. Prayer for continued protection and justice (10–12\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### God and man

Evil people do not think about God; but he is such a pleasure to all who honor him.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 36:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 36:0 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_i0eu)

לַ⁠מְנַצֵּ֬חַ

**"QUOTE\_NOT\_FOUND: לַ⁠מְנַצֵּ֬חַ"**

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: \[For the music director] or \[For the leader of worship music]
