## Psalms - Chapter 83 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_kij7)

Psalm 83 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 83 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It is such a desperate, urgent plea for help that it presents only three of the basic elements of that type of psalm. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1\)
2. Description of troubles (2–8\)
3. Petition (9–18\)

Many interpreters believe that this psalm was written during the reign of Jehoshaphat when a large army composed of Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites, supported by other nations, invaded and attacked Judah, as described in 2 Chronicles 20:1–30\. Yahweh inspired a Levite from the clan of Asaph to reassure the king and nation that he would defeat these invaders. The outcome was exactly what this psalm envisions and pleads for: “the fear of God was on all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard how Yahweh had fought with the enemies of Israel.” It may be helpful to read this passage before translating this psalm.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 83:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); Asaph (ID: `person:Asaph.2`)

## Psalms - Chapter 84 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_mf13)

Psalm 84 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

While Psalm 84 is not identified explicitly in its superscription as a “song of ascents” like Psalms 120–134, it nevertheless seems to be that same type of psalm. It encourages and praises going to the temple in Jerusalem. Apparently writing from the perspective of his arrival at the temple, the psalmist describes how he longed to be there and the journey he made to get there. The superscription indicates that a Korahite Levite wrote this psalm, but it was evidently one who lived and worked at some distance from Jerusalem.

1. Celebration of the temple (1–4\)
2. The journey to the temple (5–7\)
3. Prayer for Yahweh to preserve the king (8–9\)
4. Celebration of Yahweh, the God of this temple, for his goodness (10–12\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 84:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); Korah (ID: `person:Korah.3`)

## Psalms - Chapter 85 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_vtd4)

Psalm 85 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 85 is a psalm of supplication or lament. In its core, it presents three of the basic elements of that type of psalm. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) It was most likely written shortly after the first group of Judeans returned from exile in Babylon. Its first part is a recollection of how Yahweh has begun to restore the people, and its concluding part is a vision of how he will do that comprehensively. The supplication in the middle is the psalmist’s plea to him to move the people from their difficult present into their hopeful future in light of what he has already done for them in the past.

1. Recollection of Yahweh’s restoration of the people (1–3\)
2. Cry for help (4–7\)
3. Petition (7\)
4. Statement of trust (8\)
5. Prediction of Yahweh’s future mercies (9–13\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 85:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); Korah (ID: `person:Korah.3`)

## Psalms 85:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_snae)

**"You favored your land, Yahweh; you restored the captivity of Jacob"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[You showed favor to your land, Yahweh, by restoring the captivity of your people] or \[You favored your land, Yahweh; indeed, you restored the captivity of Jacob]

## Psalms - Chapter 86 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_yms3)

Psalm 86 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 86 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It presents all of the basic elements of that type of psalm. (Some elements are repeated.) See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–4\)
2. Statement of trust (5\)
3. Cry for help (6\)
4. Statement of trust (7–10\)
5. Petition (11\)
6. Vow of praise (12–13\)
7. Description of troubles (14\)
8. Petition (15–17\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 86:0

**"for you, Yahweh, you help me and"**

David is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **have helped** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh personally is the one who helps him. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: \[you yourself, Yahweh, have helped me]

## Psalms - Chapter 87 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_l8z3)

Psalm 87 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 87 is a psalm of praise. It is a specific type of praise psalm, a “song of Zion.” See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Celebration of how Yahweh chose Zion as the place for his temple (1–3\)
2. Celebration of how people from all nations will worship Yahweh (4–6\)
3. Celebration of how Yahweh’s presence in Zion blesses people (7\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 87:0

The word **sons** refers to the descendants of Korah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Of those who are descended from Korah]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 87:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); Korah (ID: `person:Korah.3`); Foundation (ID: `realia:Foundation`)

## Psalms - Chapter 88 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_w2mk)

Psalm 88 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 88 is a psalm of supplication or lament. Because the psalmist is feeling such despair, he does not make a statement of trust or a vow of praise, and he does not even make a petition. (The psalmist observes instead in verses 10–12 that if Yahweh does not heal him, he will not be able to praise him.) So only two of the basic elements of a psalm of supplication are present. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry for help (1–2\)
2. Description of troubles (3–8\)
3. Cry for help (9–14\)
4. Description of troubles (15–18\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Who wrote this psalm?

The superscription to Psalm 88 says that it is both a “psalm of the sons of Korah” and a “maskil of Heman the Ezrahite.” The explanation for this is probably that the first part of the superscription belongs at the end of Psalm 87 (whose superscription attributes it to “the sons of Korah”). See the discussion of this in the introduction to the book of Psalms. As that discussion indicates, there is significant movement among biblical scholars toward seeing the musical instructions at the start of many psalm inscriptions as subscriptions to the previous psalms. However, published versions of the Bible do not yet tend to present them that way. Unless there is a Bible translation in your region that does, we recommend that you follow the current approach and retain both attributions in this superscription. The UST models one way to do that.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 88:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Ezrahites (ID: `group:Ezrahites`); Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); Heman (ID: `person:Heman`); Korah (ID: `person:Korah.3`)

## Psalms - Chapter 89 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_aw17)

Psalm 89 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 89 is a psalm of supplication or lament. It appears to have been written shortly after the destruction of Jerusalem to protest that while Yahweh had promised that David’s descendants would always rule as kings, and Yahweh had the power to make sure that happened, he allowed enemies to destroy Jerusalem and depose the king. The psalmist uses three of the basic elements of a psalm of supplication. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) However, before he does that, the psalmist praises Yahweh for his power, and he cites his covenant with David as grounds for praying for restoration. These two first parts of the psalm correspond roughly to the other two basic elements of a psalm of supplication, a vow of praise and a statement of trust.

1. Praise of Yahweh’s power and greatness (1–18\)
2. Yahweh’s covenant with David (19–37\)
3. Description of troubles (38–45\)
4. Cry for help (46–49\)
5. Petition (50–51\)

Verse 52 is not part of the original psalm. It is a doxology (an expression of praise to God) that the editors of the book of Psalms added to mark the end of Book Three of the psalms. See how you translated the similar doxologies in 41:13 and 72:18–20\.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 89:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Ezrahites (ID: `group:Ezrahites`); Ethan (ID: `person:Ethan`)

## Psalms - Chapter 90 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_gmu6)

Psalm 90 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 90 is a “wisdom psalm.” It instructs people how to be wise by honoring Yahweh and obeying him. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the Introduction to Psalms.)

This psalm is a poem, the words to a song, and so the ULT sets its lines farther to the right on the page than ordinary text in order to show that they are poetry.

1. God’s eternity and human mortality (1–6\)
2. People perish when God punishes them for sin (7–12\)
3. A prayer for God’s mercy and favor (13–17\)

The first part of verse 1, “A prayer of Moses, the man of God,” is the superscription to this psalm. Format it in the way that you have decided to format the other superscriptions in the book of Psalms.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Singular “you” and “your”

The pronouns “you” and “your” are singular throughout this psalm because Moses is addressing Yahweh directly. So use the singular forms of those pronouns in your translation if your language marks a distinction between singular and plural “you.”

### Exclusive “we,” “us,” and “our”

The pronouns “we,” “us,” and “our” are exclusive throughout this psalm because Moses is speaking to Yahweh on behalf of the Israelites. So use the exclusive forms of those pronouns in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:0

Moses is speaking as if the **mountains** on earth had actually been **born** and as if God had actually **brought forth**, that is, given birth to, the **earth** and the **world**. He means that God created these things. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Before you created the mountains or formed the earth and the world]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:2
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 90:2 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_mz45)

אֶ֣רֶץ וְ⁠תֵבֵ֑ל

**"the earth and the world"**

The terms **earth** and **world** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: \[the entire earth]

See: Doublet

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:2
* **Associated Articles:** Doublet (ID: `33266@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 90:2 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_x21e)

וּֽ⁠מֵ⁠עוֹלָ֥ם עַד־ע֝וֹלָ֗ם

**"even from forever to forever"**

Moses is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, eternity past and eternity future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: \[throughout all of time]

See: Merism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:2
* **Associated Articles:** Merism (ID: `33291@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 90:2 (#5) (id: en_tn_PSA_p613)

אַתָּ֥ה אֵֽל

**"you {are} God"**

As the ULT indicates by using brackets, the verb here is understood, so translators must decide what tense best fits the context. It would be conventional in many languages to use the past tense when describing something that was true a long time ago, so many languages might ordinarily say “you were God.” But Moses means that Yahweh was God long ago, that he is God now, and that he will continue to be God forever into the future. To convey this, the ULT uses the present tense, saying **you are God**. Decide what tense would best convey the meaning in your own language.

See: Irregular Use of Tenses

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:2
* **Associated Articles:** Irregular Use of Tenses (ID: `33403@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 90:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_spk9)

תָּשֵׁ֣ב אֱ֭נוֹשׁ עַד־דַּכָּ֑א וַ֝⁠תֹּ֗אמֶר שׁ֣וּבוּ בְנֵי־אָדָֽם

**"You cause man to return to dust, and you say, “Return, sons of man"**

Moses is describing one event, **man** returning to **dust**, before describing another event that preceded it, God telling him to do that. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: \[You say, “Return, sons of man,” and you cause man to return to dust]

See: Order of Events

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:3
* **Associated Articles:** Order of Events (ID: `33269@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 90:3 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_yjk2)

אֱ֭נוֹשׁ

**"man"**

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: \[people]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:3
* **Associated Articles:** Generic Noun Phrases (ID: `33277@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 90:3 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_j396)

תָּשֵׁ֣ב אֱ֭נוֹשׁ עַד־דַּכָּ֑א \& שׁ֣וּבוּ

**"You cause man to return to dust \& Return"**

Moses is using the expression **return to dust** to mean “die.” It is an allusion to the way that God formed the first man from the dust of the ground, as described in Genesis 2:7\. This is one of several mild or poetic ways in which Moses refers to death in this psalm. Your language may have a similar expression that you can use here in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: \[You cause people to pass away… Pass away] or \[You cause people to die … It is time for you to die]

See: Euphemism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:3
* **Associated Articles:** Euphemism (ID: `33268@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 90:3 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_b3dr)

בְנֵי־אָדָֽם

**"sons of man"**

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[human beings]

See: Idiom

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:3
* **Associated Articles:** Idiom (ID: `33283@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 90:4 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_b3xf)

כִּ֤י

**"For"**

Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an affirmation. Alternate translation: \[Indeed]

* **Associated Articles:** Connecting Words and Phrases (ID: `33335@UWTranslationManual`)

בְּֽ⁠עֵינֶ֗י⁠ךָ

**"in your eyes"**

Moses is using the common expression of his culture **in your eyes** to mean “in your perspective.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[in your perspective]

See: Idiom

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:4
* **Associated Articles:** Idiom (ID: `33283@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 90:4 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_zt2t)

כְּ⁠י֣וֹם אֶ֭תְמוֹל כִּ֣י יַעֲבֹ֑ר וְ⁠אַשְׁמוּרָ֥ה בַ⁠לָּֽיְלָה

**"are} like the day before when it has passed, and a watch in the night"**

The point of these comparisons is that both of the times that Moses mentions seem very short to people: **the day before**, once it is over, and a **watch in the night** that lasts only a few hours. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: \[seem very short, like yesterday, when it is over, or like a three\-hour watch in the night]

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:4
* **Associated Articles:** Simile (ID: `33314@UWTranslationManual`)

The pronoun **them** refers to people, that is, to the “sons of man” whom Moses mentions in verse 3, not to the “thousand years” that he mentions in verse 4\. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: \[You flood people away]

זְ֭רַמְתָּ⁠ם

**"You flood them away"**

Moses is speaking as if God actually used a **flood** of water to sweep people **away** from the earth. He is using the image to convey the idea that God may cause people to die suddenly, unexpectedly, and with no recourse. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. שֵׁנָ֣ה יִהְי֑וּ

**"they are sleep"**

Moses is speaking as if people were actually **sleep**. This could mean: (1\) that Moses is using the term **sleep** as a mild way of referring to death. Alternate translation: \[then they are dead] or (2\) that Moses is illustrating the brevity of human life by comparing it to **sleep** that lasts only a few hours and then is over. Alternate translation: \[their lives are short, like a few hours of sleep that soon end]

**"like grass, it passes along"**

The point of this comparison is that just as grass **passes along** through its brief cycle of life, so human life lasts for only a short time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: \[A person’s life is short, like grass that quickly passes along]

## Psalms 90:6 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_gmeb)

בַּ֭⁠בֹּקֶר יָצִ֣יץ וְ⁠חָלָ֑ף לָ֝⁠עֶ֗רֶב יְמוֹלֵ֥ל וְ⁠יָבֵֽשׁ

**"In the morning it sprouts and passes along; in the evening it withers and dries up"**

Moses says that grass lives for only a single day, lasting only from **morning** to **evening**, as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: \[Grass blossoms and grows for only a short time; very soon it withers and dries up]

* **Associated Articles:** Hyperbole (ID: `33281@UWTranslationManual`)

יְמוֹלֵ֥ל וְ⁠יָבֵֽשׁ

**"it withers and dries up"**

The terms **withers** and **dries up** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: \[it dries up completely]

* **Associated Articles:** Doublet (ID: `33266@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 90:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_vhb5)

כִּֽי־כָלִ֥ינוּ בְ⁠אַפֶּ֑⁠ךָ וּֽ⁠בַ⁠חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֥ נִבְהָֽלְנוּ

**"For by your nose, we perish, and by your wrath we are terrified"**

Moses is referring to God’s **nose** as a common expression of his culture to mean God’s anger. Your language and culture may also associate anger with a particular part of the body. If so, in your translation you could use an expression involving that part of the body. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: \[by your anger we perish, and by your wrath we are terrified]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 90:7
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 90:7 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_lcdl)

כִּֽי־כָלִ֥ינוּ בְ⁠אַפֶּ֑⁠ךָ וּֽ⁠בַ⁠חֲמָתְ⁠ךָ֥ נִבְהָֽלְנוּ

**"For by your nose, we perish, and by your wrath we are terrified"**

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to reverse the order of the phrases, since people would first be **terrified** by God’s **wrath** and then they would **perish** when he destroyed them in his anger. ## Psalms 90:8 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_bv82)

שַׁתָּ֣ה עֲוֺנֹתֵ֣י⁠נוּ לְ⁠נֶגְדֶּ֑⁠ךָ עֲ֝לֻמֵ֗⁠נוּ לִ⁠מְא֥וֹר פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ

**"You have set our iniquities before you, our hidden {sin} in the light of your face"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[You have studied our iniquities, yes, you have carefully examined our hidden sin]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 90:8 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_fbk1)

שַׁתָּ֣ה עֲוֺנֹתֵ֣י⁠נוּ לְ⁠נֶגְדֶּ֑⁠ךָ

**"You have set our iniquities before you"**

Moses is speaking as if God had actually **set** the **iniquities** of the Israelites in front of him where he could see them. The idea is that God is paying attention to the wrong things that the Israelites have done, and God is punishing them for doing those things, as the previous verse indicates. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[You examine our iniquities]

## Psalms - Chapter 91 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_ye5h)

Psalm 91 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 91 is a “psalm of trust.” (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the General Introduction to Psalms.)

This psalm is a poem, the words to a song, and so the ULT sets its lines farther to the right on the page than ordinary text in order to show that they are poetry.

1. The psalmist describes how Yahweh protects those who trust him (1–13\)
2. Yahweh describes how he protects those who trust him (14–16\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Singular “you” and “your”

The pronouns “you” and “your” are singular in verses 1–13 because the psalmist is speaking individually to people whom he wants to encourage to trust Yahweh. So use the singular forms of those pronouns in your translation if your language marks a distinction between singular and plural “you.”

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 91:0


## Psalms 91:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_lc6j)

**"The one dwelling in the shelter of the Most High"**

The psalmist is speaking as if the **Most High**, that is, God, were actually a **shelter** in which a person could live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[The one who depends on the Most High for protection]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 91:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

**"You will tread on the lion and the adder; you will trample the young lion and the serpent"**

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **lion**, **adder**, **young lion**, or **serpent**. He means such animals in general. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using plural forms. Alternate translation: \[You will tread on lions and adders; you will trample young lions and serpents]

See: Generic Noun Phrases

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 91:13
* **Associated Articles:** Generic Noun Phrases (ID: `33277@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Lion (ID: `fauna:Lion`); Snake (ID: `fauna:Snake`); Cobra (ID: `fauna:Cobra`); Dragon (ID: `fauna:Dragon`)

## Psalms 91:13 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_qme2)

עַל־שַׁ֣חַל וָ⁠פֶ֣תֶן תִּדְרֹ֑ךְ תִּרְמֹ֖ס כְּפִ֣יר וְ⁠תַנִּֽין

**"You will tread on the lion and the adder; you will trample the young lion and the serpent"**

The psalmist may be using the terms **tread** and **trample** to mean “defeat.” People in this culture would force defeated enemies to lie down and then place a foot on top of them to show how completely they had defeated them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[You will defeat any lion or adder that attacks you; yes, you will defeat any young lion or serpent that attacks you]

See: Metonymy

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 91:13
* **Associated Articles:** Metonymy (ID: `33293@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Lion (ID: `fauna:Lion`); Snake (ID: `fauna:Snake`); Cobra (ID: `fauna:Cobra`); Dragon (ID: `fauna:Dragon`)

## Psalms 91:13 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_sw74)

**"You will tread on the lion and the adder; you will trample the young lion and the serpent"**

The psalmist is using a hypothetical situation to help the individual he is addressing appreciate how Yahweh will protect him. Use a natural form in your language for expressing a hypothetical situation. To do that, it may be helpful to combine the two parallel phrases in this verse. Alternate translation: \[Suppose a lion or a snake attacks you. ## Psalms - Chapter 92 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_cs72)

Psalm 92 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 92 is a psalm of praise for God’s kindness and faithfulness. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]])

1. It is good to praise the Lord (1–4\)
2. God’s works are great and his ways are deep (5–9\)
3. God strengthens and honors the righteous (10–11\)
4. The righteous will flourish (12–15\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Justice

God causes evil people to be destroyed and good people to be happy and useful, even after they grow old. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 92:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Sabbath (ID: `keyterm:Sabbath`); Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`)

## Psalms - Chapter 93 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_r2fh)

Psalm 93 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 93 is a “worship psalm” about the power of Yahweh.

1. Yahweh reigns in glory and strength (1–2\)
2. Yahweh is stronger than chaos and opposition (3–4\)
3. Yahweh is trustworthy and holy (5\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s power

Yahweh is all powerful; He even controls the ocean.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 93:0

Verses 1 and 4 of this psalm refer to Yahweh as “he” and verses 2,3, and 5 refer to him as “you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use “you” throughout the psalm, as in the UST.

See: First, Second or Third Person

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 93:1
* **Associated Articles:** First, Second or Third Person (ID: `33256@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 94 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_afb5)

Psalm 94 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 94 is a prayer requesting that evil people be punished. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

1. A cry for Yahweh’s justice (1–7\)
2. Yahweh sees and will judge (8–11\)
3. Yahweh disciplines and helps his people (12–15\)
4. Yahweh is the refuge of the oppressed (16–23\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Justice

Evil people expect God to ignore their injustices. But God knows what they are doing and will punish them for their evil deeds. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 94:0


## Psalms 94:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_zdpn)

**"God of vengeance, Yahweh, God of vengeance"**

Here, **God of vengeance, Yahweh, God of vengeance** the psalmist is using repetition for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh, the God who avenges]

See: Poetry

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 94:1
* **Associated Articles:** Poetry (ID: `33422@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

* **Associated Articles:** Abstract Nouns (ID: `33257@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 94:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_s0ov)

עַד־מָתַ֖י רְשָׁעִ֥ים ׀ יְהוָ֑ה עַד־מָ֝תַ֗י רְשָׁעִ֥ים יַעֲלֹֽזוּ

**"Until when will the wicked, Yahweh, until when will the wicked rejoice"**

The psalmist is using the question form **Until when will the wicked, Yahweh, until when will the wicked rejoice** to express his frustration and to make an urgent appeal to God for action. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh, the wicked have been rejoicing much too long.]

## Psalms 94:16 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_ql5m)

מִֽי־יָק֣וּם לִ֭⁠י עִם־מְרֵעִ֑ים מִֽי־יִתְיַצֵּ֥ב לִ֝⁠י עִם־פֹּ֥עֲלֵי אָֽוֶן

**"Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? Who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness"**

These two phrases **Who will rise up for me against the evildoers** and **Who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? I say again, who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 94:16
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Mischief (ID: `keyterm:Mischief`)

## Psalms - Chapter 95 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_e91f)

Psalm 95 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 95 is the first in a series of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100\).

1. Call to worship (1–5\)
2. Call to bow in worship (6–7a)
3. Warning to listen and obey (7b–11\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### God’s care

God made everything and takes good care of people. People should not be stubborn, as the Israelites were in the days of Moses. The Israelites with Moses wandered in the desert for 40 years.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 95:0

## Psalms - Chapter 96 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_hdp3)

Psalm 96 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 96 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100\).

1. Call to sing and declare Yahweh’s greatness (1–6\)
2. Call the nations to worship (7–9\)
3. Yahweh’s reign and coming judgment (10–13\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh, the king

Yahweh is king over all the earth and is worthy of all praise.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 96:0

## Psalms - Chapter 97 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_ydx4)

Psalm 97 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 97 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100\).

1. Yahweh reigns in power and glory (1–6\)
2. Idols are exposed as worthless (7–9\)
3. The righteous are called to love and rejoice in Yahweh (10–12\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s authority

All people who worship idols are disgraced because Yahweh rules over all the world.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 97:0

## Psalms 97:7 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_hx36)

הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ־ל֝⁠וֹ כָּל־אֱלֹהִֽים

**"bow down to him, all you gods"**

The psalmist has been addressing his audience, but now he briefly addresses **all you gods**, even though he knows that these gods cannot hear him. He does this in order to express more powerfully his feelings about Yahweh’s supremacy over all other so\-called gods. If it would be helpful in your language, you could introduce this more clearly and put the rest of this address in quote marks. Alternate translation: \[I would tell those worthless idols to bow down to him]

## Psalms - Chapter 98 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_rt9w)

Psalm 98 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 98 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100\).

1. Sing a new song for Yahweh’s saving work (1–3\)
2. Shout and rejoice in worship (4–6\)
3. All creation celebrates Yahweh’s righteous rule (7–9\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Praise

Everyone and every thing should sing praises to Yahweh because he is worthy of all praise.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 98:0

Here, **his right hand and the arm of his holiness** represents God’s great power. The psalmist is using body parts to refer to God’s strength and ability to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[his great and holy power]

See: Metonymy

## Psalms - Chapter 99 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_wma5)

Psalm 99 Introduction
=====================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 99 is one of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100\).

1. Yahweh reigns over all peoples (1–3\)
2. Yahweh loves justice and rules rightly (4–5\)
3. Yahweh answers his faithful servants (6–9\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s justice

God is just and fair. Moses, Aaron and Samuel each prayed to him and obeyed him, and he answered their prayers. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/justice]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 99:0


## Psalms 99:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_x0pi)

**"Yahweh reigns—let the peoples tremble— sitting {above} the cherubim; let the earth quake"**

If it would be helpful in your language, you could move the phrase **let the peoples tremble** so that it does not interrupt the larger sentence. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh reigns, sitting above the cherubim; let the peoples tremble and let the earth quake]

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 99:1

## Psalms - Chapter 100 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_n9yp)

Psalm 100 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 100 is the last of this group of six “worship psalms” (Psalms 95–100\).

1. Call to joyful praise (1–2\)
2. Reason for worship: Yahweh is God (3\)
3. Enter with thanksgiving and praise (4\)
4. Yahweh’s character is the foundation of praise (5\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s care for his creation

God made mankind and takes good care of people.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 100:0

**"Shout to Yahweh"**

The command forms such as **shout** are plural in this psalm because the psalmist is calling all people to praise God, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. See how “shout” is translated in Psalms 47:1\. Alternate translation: \[Raise a shout to Yahweh]

See: Forms of ‘You’ — Singular

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 100:1
* **Associated Articles:** Forms of ‘You’ — Singular (ID: `33321@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); Praise (ID: `keyterm:Praise`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 101 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_vhm3)

Psalm 101 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 101 is a psalm of David asking God’s help to live as a person should. With God’s help, David pledges to rule uprightly and to get rid of all evildoers.

1. David commits to upright life (1–2\)
2. David rejects evil and deceit (3–7\)
3. David promises justice and faithfulness (8\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Encouragement

David wanted to encourage all the good people in the land and restrain all the evil people. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 101:0


## Psalms 101:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_fcvq)

אָשִׁ֑ירָה

**"I shall sing"**

See the introduction to Psalms for an explanation of the word **shall**.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 101:1

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`); Kindness (ID: `keyterm:Kindness`)

See: Abstract Nouns

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 101:1
* **Associated Articles:** Abstract Nouns (ID: `33257@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`); Kindness (ID: `keyterm:Kindness`)

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

## Psalms 101:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_dxv4)

לֹֽא־יֵשֵׁ֨ב ׀ בְּ⁠קֶ֥רֶב בֵּיתִ⁠י֮ עֹשֵׂ֪ה רְמִ֫יָּ֥ה דֹּבֵ֥ר שְׁקָרִ֑ים לֹֽא־יִ֝כּ֗וֹן לְ⁠נֶ֣גֶד עֵינָֽ⁠י

**"A doer of deceit will not remain within my house; a speaker of lies will not be established before my eyes"**

These two phrases **A doer of deceit will not remain within my house** and **a speaker of lies will not be established before my eyes** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[A doer of deceit will not remain within my house, no, a speaker of lies will not be established before my eyes]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms - Chapter 102 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_ew2b)

Psalm 102 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 102 is a “lament.”

1. Cry of distress and plea for mercy (1–11\)
2. Confidence in Yahweh’s eternal purposes and mercy (12–17\)
3. Call to record and remember Yahweh’s mercies (18–22\)
4. Yahweh sustains and remains unchanging (23–28\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Salvation

The psalmist does not want to die young. He also wants to see Jerusalem saved. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 102:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 102:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_n78t)

יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְעָ֣⁠ה תְפִלָּתִ֑⁠י וְ֝⁠שַׁוְעָתִ֗⁠י אֵלֶ֥י⁠ךָ תָבֽוֹא

**"Hear my prayer, Yahweh; let my cry come unto you"**

These two phrases **Hear my prayer, Yahweh** and **let my cry come unto you** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: \[Hear my prayer, Yahweh, as I cry out to you]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 102:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

**"Hear my prayer"**

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: \[Please hear my prayer]

See: Imperatives — Other Uses

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 102:1
* **Associated Articles:** Imperatives — Other Uses (ID: `33284@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 102:2 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_zstb)

## Psalms 102:6 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_e04t)

לִ⁠קְאַ֣ת

**"an owl"**

The word translated as “owl” here is obscure. Most scholars believe that the word refers to a type of owl. The ancient Greek translation used the word for “pelican” here, and that was followed by some older versions, although a pelican is a water bird that cannot live in a dry wilderness. If “pelican” is correct, then the psalmist is saying that he feels as though he is living in a place where he cannot survive. If “owl” is correct, then the psalmist is saying that he feels alone and abandoned. You may want to use the word that the major translation in your area uses.

See: Translate Unknowns

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 102:6
* **Associated Articles:** Translate Unknowns (ID: `33408@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 102:13 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_uxs0)

תָ֭קוּם

**"you will arise"**

The psalmist is using **you will arise** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that God is about to begin taking action to help his people. He does not mean that God is getting out of bed or standing up from a seated position. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[you will go into action] or \[you will do something]

See: Idiom

## Psalms 102:17 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_u228)

פָּ֭נָה אֶל־תְּפִלַּ֣ת הָ⁠עַרְעָ֑ר וְ⁠לֹֽא־בָ֝זָ֗ה אֶת־תְּפִלָּתָֽ⁠ם

**"He turns to the prayer of the destitute and he does not despise their prayer"**

These two phrases **He turns to the prayer of the destitute** and **he does not despise their prayer** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[He turns to the prayer of the destitute; certainly, he does not despise their prayer]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 102:17
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 102:17
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated Articles:** Possession (ID: `33303@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 102:17 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_ww7b)

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **despise**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: \[and he accepts their prayer]

## Psalms 102:26 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_bzq7)

הֵ֤מָּה ׀ יֹאבֵדוּ֮

**"They, they will perish"**

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **they will perish** already contains that meaning. He is doing that for emphasis because he is contrasting the earth and heavens (which will perish) with God (who will remain). If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: \[As for them, they will perish]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 102:26
* **Associated Articles:** Pronouns — When to Use Them (ID: `33424@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms - Chapter 103 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_b1ht)

Psalm 103 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 103 is the first in a series of five “psalm of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107\).

1. Call to bless Yahweh with whole being (1–2\)
2. Yahweh’s forgiveness, healing, and provision (3–5\)
3. Yahweh’s compassionate character (6–14\)
4. Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness from everlasting (15–22\)
5. Yahweh’s sovereign rule over all (19–22\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s grace

God shows his goodness to us by forgiving our sins and not punishing us as much as we deserve.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 103:0


## Psalms 103:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_bk7g)

בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁ⁠י אֶת־יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠כָל־קְ֝רָבַ֗⁠י אֶת־שֵׁ֥ם קָדְשֽׁ⁠וֹ

**"Bless Yahweh, my soul! And all of my inward parts, the name of his holiness"**

The phrases **Bless Yahweh, my soul** and **all of my inward parts, the name of his holiness** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Bless Yahweh, my soul! Yes, all of my inward parts, bless the name of his holiness]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 103:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Bless (ID: `keyterm:Bless`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 103:10 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_kibv)

לֹ֣א כַ֭⁠חֲטָאֵי⁠נוּ עָ֣שָׂה לָ֑⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א כַ֝⁠עֲוֺנֹתֵ֗י⁠נוּ גָּמַ֥ל עָלֵֽי⁠נוּ

**"He does not deal with us according to our sins, and he does not treat us according to our iniquities"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as in the UST. Otherwise, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[He does not deal with us according to our sins; let me say again, he does not treat us according to our iniquities]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 103:10
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** To Sin (ID: `keyterm:Sin`); Passion (ID: `keyterm:Ardour`)

## Psalms 103:10 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_w3ov)

לֹ֣א כַ֭⁠חֲטָאֵי⁠נוּ עָ֣שָׂה לָ֑⁠נוּ וְ⁠לֹ֥א כַ֝⁠עֲוֺנֹתֵ֗י⁠נוּ גָּמַ֥ל עָלֵֽי⁠נוּ

**"He does not deal with us according to our sins, and he does not treat us according to our iniquities"**

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that people’s sins and iniquities deserve punishment from God. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: \[He does not give punishment to us that is as bad as our sins, and he does not treat us as badly as our iniquities deserve]

See: Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 103:10
* **Associated Articles:** Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information (ID: `33273@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** To Sin (ID: `keyterm:Sin`); Passion (ID: `keyterm:Ardour`)

## Psalms 103:11 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_jont)

כִּ֤י כִ⁠גְבֹ֣הַּ שָׁ֭מַיִם עַל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ גָּבַ֥ר חַ֝סְדּ֗⁠וֹ עַל־יְרֵאָֽי⁠ו

**"For as the heavens are high above the earth, his covenant faithfulness is strong toward those fearing him"**

If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: \[For just as it is impossible to measure how high the heavens are above the earth, it is also impossible to measure how strong his covenant faithfulness is toward those fearing him]

## Psalms - Chapter 104 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_zu7w)

Psalm 104 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 104 is the second in the series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107\).

1. Yahweh’s greatness in creation (1–6\)
2. Yahweh’s sustaining care over creation (7–30\)
3. Yahweh’s glory declared forever (31–32\)
4. Everlasting praise to Yahweh (33–35\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s creation

God has created everything good on earth, in the sky, and in the sea.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 104:0

## Psalms 104:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_uwav)

מִן־גַּעֲרָ֣תְ⁠ךָ֣ יְנוּס֑וּ⁠ן מִן־ק֥וֹל רַֽ֝עַמְ⁠ךָ֗ יֵחָפֵזֽוּ⁠ן

**"From your rebuke they fled; from your voice of thunder they hurried away"**

These two phrases **From your rebuke they fled** and **from your voice of thunder they hurried away** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could combine the phrases. Alternate translation: \[From your thunderous rebuke they fled away]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 104:7
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 104:8 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ba9m)

יַעֲל֣וּ הָ֭רִים יֵרְד֣וּ בְקָע֑וֹת

**"They ascended the mountains; they descended the valleys"**

**They** refers to “the waters” from verse 6\. This reflects the idea from Genesis 7:11 that the flood waters came from where they had been stored both above the firmament and underground. Here it is saying that after the flood God returned the waters to those places, so some of it **ascended the mountains** to return to the heavens and some **descended the valleys** to return to their places underground.

**"They ascended the mountains; they descended the valleys"**

Some translations take **the mountains** to be the subject of **ascended** and **the valleys** to be the subject of **descended**. This makes it difficult to translate the following verse however, since verse 9 continues to refer to the waters as “they.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to follow what it does here. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to follow the ULT. Alternate translation: \[The mountains rose; the valleys descended]

## Psalms - Chapter 105 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_lfu2)

Psalm 105 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 105 is the third in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107\). Psalm 105 retells the history of Israel from Yahweh’s covenant with Abraham, to the people’s enslavement in Egypt, to Yahweh’s liberation of the people through the plagues in Egypt, to Yahweh giving them the land of Canaan.

1. Praise Yahweh and seek his works (1–6\)
2. Yahweh’s covenant and deeds with the patriarchs (7–15\)
3. Yahweh’s guidance over Joseph and Israel in Egypt (16–25\)
4. Yahweh’s deliverance and provision in the wilderness (26–45\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s protection

God protected Abraham and Jacob. He worked throughout Israel’s history to bring Israel into the land he had promised them. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 105:0

## Psalms 105:8 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_m5jl)

**"He remembers his covenant forever, the word he commanded for a thousand generations"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[He remembers his covenant forever, yes, the word he commanded for a thousand generations]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 105:8
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 105:23 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_i862)

וַ⁠יָּבֹ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל מִצְרָ֑יִם וְ֝⁠יַעֲקֹ֗ב גָּ֣ר בְּ⁠אֶֽרֶץ־חָֽם

**"Then Israel came into Egypt, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Then Israel came into Egypt; yes, Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 105:23
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. ## Psalms - Chapter 106 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_b2l3)

Psalm 106 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 106 is the fourth in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107\). The book of Psalms is divided into five sections, also called “books,” and Psalm 106 ends book four. Verses 47 and 48 are considered to be a closing petition and praise for book four, rather than belonging specifically to Psalm 106\.

1. Praise Yahweh for his goodness and faithfulness (1–3\)
2. Plea for pardon and Yahweh’s acceptance (4–6\)
3. Recount Israel’s rebellion and Yahweh’s mercy (7–46\)
4. Prayer and praise to Yahweh (47–48\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Israel’s sin

Although Israel continually sinned in the desert, God still took them to the Promised Land. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sin]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 106:0

## Psalms 106:10 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ikvr)

These two phrases **he saved them from the hand of the hater** and **he rescued them from the hand of the enemy** mean basically the same thing. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. **"So he said to annihilate them"**

The implication is that God was determined to destroy the Israelites because of their sin, but Moses interceded for them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: \[So he intended to annihilate them] or \[So he would have annihilated them]

* **Associated Articles:** Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information (ID: `33273@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms 106:23 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_hxj5)

לוּלֵ֡י מֹ֘שֶׁ֤ה בְחִיר֗⁠וֹ עָמַ֣ד בַּ⁠פֶּ֣רֶץ

**"had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach"**

The psalmist says **had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach** to introduce a situation that did not happen in order to help explain what would have happened if Moses had not interceded for the Israelites. Use a natural method in your language for introducing a situation that did not happen. Alternate translation: \[if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood in the breach]

If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: \[the one whom God had chosen]

## Psalms 106:27 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_uboe)

וּ⁠לְ⁠הַפִּ֣יל זַ֭רְעָ⁠ם בַּ⁠גּוֹיִ֑ם וּ֝⁠לְ⁠זָרוֹתָ֗⁠ם בָּ⁠אֲרָצֽוֹת

**"and to make their seed fall among the nations, and to scatter them among the lands"**

These two phrases **to make their seed fall among the nations** and **to scatter them among the lands** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: \[and to scatter their descendants among people of foreign lands]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 106:27

**"they rebelled against his spirit"**

Other ancient manuscripts read “they embittered his spirit.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. ## Psalms 106:35 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_wkcs)

וַ⁠יִּתְעָרְב֥וּ בַ⁠גּוֹיִ֑ם

**"but they mingled with the nations"**

The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites had **mingled** or mixed themselves physically with the nations. He means that they intermarried with people from other nations and adopted their religious and cultural practices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[but they intermarried with people of the nations]

## Psalms 106:39 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_wvd4)

וַ⁠יִּטְמְא֥וּ בְ⁠מַעֲשֵׂי⁠הֶ֑ם וַ֝⁠יִּזְנוּ֗ בְּ⁠מַֽעַלְלֵי⁠הֶֽם

**"And they became unclean by their deeds; and they prostituted themselves by their actions"**

These two phrases **And they became unclean by their deeds** and **and they prostituted themselves by their actions** mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[And they became unclean by their deeds; indeed, they prostituted themselves by their actions]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 106:39
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Defilement (ID: `keyterm:Defilement`); Play the Prostitute (ID: `keyterm:PlayTheProstitute`)

## Psalms 106:39 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_k3ty)

וַ⁠יִּטְמְא֥וּ

**"And they became unclean"**

The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites had **become unclean** physically through their sinful actions. He means that they became spiritually defiled or morally corrupted by their idolatrous practices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[And they became very sinful]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 106:39
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Defilement (ID: `keyterm:Defilement`); Play the Prostitute (ID: `keyterm:PlayTheProstitute`)

## Psalms 106:39 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_o80r)

וַ֝⁠יִּזְנוּ֗

**"and they prostituted themselves"**

The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites were unfaithful wives who **prostituted themselves**. He means that they violated their covenant relationship with Yahweh by worshiping idols. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[and they violated their relationship with Yahweh]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 106:39
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Defilement (ID: `keyterm:Defilement`); Play the Prostitute (ID: `keyterm:PlayTheProstitute`)

## Psalms 106:42 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_hfts)

וַ⁠יִּלְחָצ֥וּ⁠ם אוֹיְבֵי⁠הֶ֑ם וַ֝⁠יִּכָּנְע֗וּ תַּ֣חַת יָדָֽ⁠ם

These two phrases **And their enemies oppressed them** and **and they were humbled under their hand** mean basically the same thing. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. ## Psalms 106:43 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_z8en)

וְ֭⁠הֵמָּה יַמְר֣וּ

**"but they, they were rebellious"**

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they were rebellious** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between God’s repeated rescue and the people’s persistent rebellion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. ## Psalms - Chapter 107 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_j88n)

Psalm 107 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 107 is the last in a series of five “psalms of praise” to God (Psalm 103–107\).

1. A call to thanksgiving (1–3\)
2. Stories of Yahweh’s deliverance (4–32\)
3. Yahweh’s transformative power (33–41\)
4. A final exhortation (42–43\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Praise

The psalmist praises Yahweh for saving people lost in the desert, in prison, sick, in a storm at sea, homeless and oppressed. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 107:0

These two phrases **had rebelled against the words of God** and **despised the counsel of the Most High** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[they had rebelled against the words of God, indeed, they had despised the counsel of the Most High]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 107:11
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Rebel (ID: `keyterm:Rebel`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); Counsel (ID: `keyterm:Counsel`)

יָשֵׂ֣ם מִ֭דְבָּר לַֽ⁠אֲגַם־מַ֑יִם וְ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צִ֝יָּ֗ה לְ⁠מֹצָ֥אֵי מָֽיִם

**"He turns the wilderness into a pool of water and dry land into springs of water"**

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: \[He turns the wilderness into a pool of water and he turns dry land into springs of water]

* **Associated Articles:** Ellipsis (ID: `33267@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 107:35 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_hyfg)

יָשֵׂ֣ם מִ֭דְבָּר לַֽ⁠אֲגַם־מַ֑יִם וְ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צִ֝יָּ֗ה לְ⁠מֹצָ֥אֵי מָֽיִם

**"He turns the wilderness into a pool of water and dry land into springs of water"**

These two phrases **He turns the wilderness into a pool of water** and **dry land into springs of water** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[He turns the wilderness into a pool of water, yes, dry land into springs of water]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 107:35
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 107:35 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_eog7)

יָשֵׂ֣ם מִ֭דְבָּר לַֽ⁠אֲגַם־מַ֑יִם וְ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צִ֝יָּ֗ה לְ⁠מֹצָ֥אֵי מָֽיִם

**"He turns the wilderness into a pool of water and dry land into springs of water"**

The psalmist says this as an overstatement for emphasis. He assumes that readers will know that only parts of the **wilderness** and **dry land** become **water**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: \[He turns many areas of the wilderness into pools of water and places springs of water throughout the dry land]

See: Hyperbole

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 107:35

## Psalms - Chapter 108 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_vpj5)

Psalm 108 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 108 is a psalm of praise and petition.

1. Praise for Yahweh’s covenant faithfulness (1–5\)
2. Yahweh’s sovereign dominion and promised kingdom (6–9\)
3. Prayer for deliverance and victory (10–13\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Victory

God affirms that he is in control of all nations, but the psalmist has not had success against his enemies. He admits that only God can give him victory, and so he asks God to give him victory over Edom.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

Verses 1–5 are very similar to Psalm 57:7–11, and verses 6–13 are very similar to Psalm 60:5–12\. If you have already translated those psalms, look at them to see how to translate this psalm.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 108:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 109 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_vpj6)

Psalm 109 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 109 is a “psalm of petition,” asking Yahweh to give David relief from his enemies who are falsely accusing him and persecuting him. He also asks Yahweh to curse these people who are enemies of both Yahweh and David.

1. Complaint and accusation (1–5\)
2. Curses against enemies (6–20\)
3. David’s plea for himself (21–29\)
4. Praise and confidence (30–31\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Cursing of Enemies

In this psalm, David takes evil very seriously and calls on Yahweh to punish those who are doing evil to himself and others so that the evil will stop. It is important to note that David does not take vengeance personally, but only calls on Yahweh to combat evil and to perform justice, as Yahweh has promised to do.

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Singular and Plural

David refers to his enemies in the singular in verses 6–19 and in the plural in the rest of the psalm. You may want to use the plural throughout the psalm, or you may want to add a footnote at verse 6 that explains that in the section of verses 6–19 David may be speaking of the leader of his enemies or he may be speaking of each one individually.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 109:0

The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: \[For the music director] or \[For the leader of worship music]

See: Translate Unknowns

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 109:1

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 109:18 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_h942)

**"and it entered into his inner being like water"**

David is making a comparison between **it entered into his inner being like water** and how deeply cursing has become part of his enemy’s character. The point of this comparison is that just as **water** penetrates thoroughly into a person when they drink, so **cursing** has penetrated deeply into this man’s inner being. ## Psalms 109:29 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_qjis)

יִלְבְּשׁ֣וּ שׂוֹטְנַ֣⁠י כְּלִמָּ֑ה וְ⁠יַעֲט֖וּ כַ⁠מְעִ֣יל בָּשְׁתָּֽ⁠ם

**"May my accusers be clothed with disgrace; may they wear their shame like a robe"**

These two phrases **May my accusers be clothed with disgrace** and **may they wear their shame like a robe** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[May my accusers be clothed with shameful disgrace as though it were a robe]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 109:29
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Robe (ID: `realia:Robe`)

## Psalms - Chapter 110 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_h1ti)

Psalm 110 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 110 is a psalm honoring the king as he becomes king and was also recognized as a prophecy about the coming messiah. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/prophet]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]])

1. The divine proclamation (1–2\)
2. The people’s response (3\)
3. The eternal priesthood (4\)
4. The king’s judgment \& victory (5–7\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### King

Yahweh will enable the king to conquer his enemies. Christ is seen as both high priest and king. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/highpriest]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 110:0

Yahweh is using **Sit at my right hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Take the place of highest honor and authority beside me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Sit with me in the honored place]

See: Idiom

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 110:1
* **Associated Articles:** Idiom (ID: `33283@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 111 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_mk5d)

Psalm 111 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 111 is a psalm of praise to God for his miracles and care. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/miracle]])

1. Call to praise (1–2\)
2. Yahweh’s majestic works (3–6\)
3. Yahweh’s trustworthy and enduring nature (7–9\)
4. Wisdom and praise (10\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s character

God is great. He has given his people food, land, and always keeps his promises to his people. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/peopleofgod]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 111:0

**"Hallelu Yah"**

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: \[Halleluia] or \[Praise Yah]

## Psalms - Chapter 112 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_s165)

Psalm 112 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 112 is a “wisdom psalm” teaching the value of a righteous life. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/wise]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]])

1. The blessings of the Yahweh\-fearing (1–3\)
2. The character and security of the upright (4–9\)
3. The contrast with the wicked (10\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Righteous people

The righteous people will be well\-known for their generosity and they will not have to worry about bad news because God is taking care of them.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 112:0


## Psalms 112:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_vi1y)

**"Hallelu Yah"**

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: \[Halleluia] or \[Praise Yah]

See: Copy or Borrow Words

## Psalms - Chapter 113 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_p4uj)

Psalm 113 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 113 is a “psalm of praise” to God for his goodness. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/good]])

1. The call to universal and eternal praise (1–3\)
2. The greatness of Yahweh’s majesty (4–6\)
3. The grace of Yahweh’s compassion (7–9\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s help

God helps the poor and gives children to the wife who cannot conceive children.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 113:0


## Psalms 113:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_q26h)

**"Hallelu Yah"**

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: \[Halleluia] or \[Praise Yah]

## Psalms 113:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_cdeo)

מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן

**"raising up the poor from the dust, he lifts the needy from the garbage"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[raising up the poor from the dust, yes, he lifts the needy from the garbage]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 113:7
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms - Chapter 114 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_vu9f)

Psalm 114 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 114 is a “psalm of praise” to God for his miracles in bringing the people of Israel to the promised land. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/miracle]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promisedland]])

1. God claims his people (1–2\)
2. Creation’s astonished response (3–6\)
3. Earth’s reverent awe (7–8\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Praise

The psalmist praises God for all the ways he helped his people in the past. This psalm references many miraculous events the Israelites experienced like the parting of the Sea of Reeds (Red Sea), the reversal of the Jordan River, bringing water from a rock, and the awe\-inspiring presence of God at Mount Sinai, with creation itself responding, as the earth trembled with, God’s power as he delivered his people from Egypt and led them to the land he had promised them.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 114:0


## Psalms 114:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_a994)

בְּ⁠צֵ֣את יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל מִ⁠מִּצְרָ֑יִם בֵּ֥ית יַ֝עֲקֹ֗ב מֵ⁠עַ֥ם לֹעֵֽז

**"When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people speaking a foreign language"**

These two phrases **When Israel went out from Egypt** and **the house of Jacob from a people speaking a foreign language** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[When Israel went out from Egypt, that is, the house of Jacob from a people speaking a foreign language]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 114:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Israel (ID: `person:Israel`); Egypt (ID: `place:Egypt`)

## Psalms 114:7 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_eyxn)

מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ מִ֝⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֗י אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַעֲקֹֽב

**"Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, from to the face of the God of Jacob"**

The psalmist has asked in the previous verse why the mountains and hills moved, so this verse provides the answer: it is because of the presence of the Lord. But this verse also is an exhortation to the people who live on the earth to tremble with respect before the powerful God of Jacob. So **earth** here probably refers both to the physical earth and to the people who live on it. You may want to use the parallel structure to bring out both meanings. Alternate translation: \[Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, you people of earth, from to the face of the God of Jacob]

See: Metonymy

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 114:7
