## Psalms 114:7 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_cafp)

מִ⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ מִ֝⁠לִּ⁠פְנֵ֗י אֱל֣וֹהַּ יַעֲקֹֽב

**"Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, from to the face of the God of Jacob"**

These two phrases **from to the face of the Lord** and **from to the face of the God of Jacob** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation as modeled in the UST. If, however, it would be more clear in your language, you could combine the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Tremble, earth, from to the face of the Lord, the mighty God of Jacob]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 114:7
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Israel (ID: `person:Israel`)

## Psalms - Chapter 115 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_it4i)

Psalm 115 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 115 is a “psalm of praise.”

1. Glory belongs to Yahweh alone (1–3\)
2. Futility of idols (4–8\)
3. Call for God’s people to trust Yahweh (9–11\)
4. Yahweh’s Faithfulness and Blessing (12–15\)
5. Life, praise, and hope in the living God (16–18\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s power

Yahweh is in heaven and is able to do whatever he wants. Idols can not do anything. Therefore, people and priests should trust Yahweh for their protection.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 115:0

The psalmist is using the repetition for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: \[Not at all to us, Yahweh]

See: Poetry

It is probable that when this psalm was sung, a leader would sing the second person exhortation parts and a chorus would sing the third\-person parts of verses 9–11\. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate the third person parts as second person. Alternate translation: \[your help and your shield]

See: First, Second or Third Person

## Psalms - Chapter 116 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_r7gl)

Psalm 116 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 116 is a “psalm of praise” for saving the psalmist’s life. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

1. Declaration of love and prayer (1–2\)
2. Recounting deliverance and finding rest (3–9\)
3. Vows, sacrifice, and public praise (10–19\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Healing

The psalmist was very sick and expected to die but God healed him. So he will pay his vow and sacrifice an offering of thanks. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/promise]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 116:0

Here, **my voice** represents the psalmist’s prayers and requests. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh hears me]

See: Metonymy

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 116:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metonymy (ID: `33293@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Love (ID: `keyterm:Love`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); Plea for Mercy (ID: `keyterm:Supplication`)

## Psalms 116:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_n33s)

אֲפָפ֤וּ⁠נִי ׀ חֶבְלֵי־מָ֗וֶת וּ⁠מְצָרֵ֣י שְׁא֣וֹל מְצָא֑וּ⁠נִי

**"The cords of death surrounded me, and the constrictions of Sheol found me"**

These two phrases **The cords of death surrounded me** and **the constrictions of Sheol found me** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[The cords of death surrounded me, indeed, the constrictions of Sheol found me]

See: Parallelism

The phrase **the son of your servant woman** adds to the meaning of **I am your servant**. In the culture of the time, the son of a servant woman was a permanent servant, without the right to go free after six years. See Exodus 21:2–4\. You could include this information if it would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: \[I am your permanent servant, the son of your servant woman]

## Psalms - Chapter 117 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_kfu1)

Psalm 117 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 117 is a “psalm of praise.”

1. Call to praise
2. Reasons to praise

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Praise

Everyone should praise God for his love and unending faithfulness. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/love]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/faithful]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 117:0


## Psalms 117:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_kxry)

הַֽלְל֣וּ אֶת־יְ֭הוָה כָּל־גּוֹיִ֑ם שַׁ֝בְּח֗וּ⁠הוּ כָּל־הָ⁠אֻמִּֽים

**"Praise Yahweh, all nations; extol him, all peoples"**

These two phrases **Praise Yahweh, all nations** and **extol him, all peoples** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Praise Yahweh, all nations; yes, extol him, all peoples]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 117:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 118 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_z9au)

Psalm 118 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 118 is a “psalm of thanksgiving” written on the occasion of a military victory. At the same time, it is a messianic psalm that looks forward to the triumph of Jesus Christ. Jesus applied Psalm 118:22 to himself (Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17\), and the apostle Peter applied it to Jesus both in a speech recorded in Acts (Acts 4:11\), and in his first letter (1 Peter 2:7\). See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to Thanksgiving (1–4\)
2. Testimony of deliverance (5–18\)
3. Messianic celebration (9–29\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Rejected stone

The psalmist praised Yahweh for rescuing him. God enabled him to overpower his enemies. The new Testament, and even Jesus himself, saw the rejected stone as a reference to the Messiah’s rejection by the Jewish leaders. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/christ]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 118:0

The psalmist is using **Yahweh is for me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh supports me” or “Yahweh is on my side.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh wants me to succeed]

See: Idiom

## Psalms - Chapter 119 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_dc52)

Psalm 119 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 119 is a “wisdom psalm” about the law of Yahweh. This psalm is an “acrostic” (see discussion in the Introduction to Psalms), an alphabetic poem with twenty\-two groups of eight verses each. Each group begins with a letter of the alphabet in the order of the Hebrew alphabet.

The psalmist uses many different words to refer to Yahweh’s message to us. You could attempt to use a different word for each term (ULT uses words such as “precepts,” “commandments,” and “law”), but most languages will not have that many, so just use the words that your language has.

1. Blessing for those who walk in Yahweh’s law (1–32\)
2. Prayer for understanding and guidance from Yahweh’s word (33–72\)
3. Comfort and hope in Yahweh’s word during affliction (73–112\)
4. Devotion to Yahweh’s law despite opposition (113–144\)
5. Cry for deliverance and life through Yahweh’s word (145–176\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### The law

The psalmist loved the law of Yahweh and was blessed by obeying it. (See: \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/love]] and \[\[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

“your word”
-----------

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist uses the phrase “your word” to refer more generally to Yahweh’s commandments, instructions, promises, and messages to us.

Request form
------------

Throughout this psalm, the psalmist is requesting things from Yahweh by using an imperative which may sound like a command in your language. If this would be impolite in your language, then use a form that would be more appropriate for addressing Yahweh with a request.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 119:0

See: Exclamations

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 119:1
* **Associated Articles:** Exclamations (ID: `33270@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Instruction (ID: `keyterm:Instruction`); Complete (ID: `keyterm:Complete`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: \[but as for me, I find joy in obeying your teaching]

## Psalms - Chapter 120 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_x4aj)

Psalm 120 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 120 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Plea for deliverance (1–2\)
2. Judgment on the deceiver (3–4\)
3. Complaint of distant dwelling (5–7\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 120:0

## Psalms - Chapter 121 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_n97g)

Psalm 121 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 121 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Confession of trust (1–2\)
2. Assurance of protection (3–6\)
3. Promise of preservation (Verses 7–8\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Multiple speakers

This psalm is a dialogue between two individuals as is made clear by the implied information in the UST. Make sure this is clear to your readers.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 121:0

## Psalms - Chapter 122 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_x7wj)

Psalm 122 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 122 one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Joy of arrival and worship (1–2\)
2. The commendation of Jerusalem (vv. 3–5\)
3. A prayer for peace and prosperity (6–9\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### “house of Yahweh”

In this psalm, the phrase “house of Yahweh” is used to talk about the temple. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state the meaning plainly.

### “Jerusalem”

Many times in this Psalm, the psalmist speaks directly to the city of Jerusalem even though it is not a person and cannot hear. He refers to Jerusalem in both the second and third person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 122:0

## Psalms - Chapter 123 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_vet5)

Psalm 123 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 123 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. The servant’s posture: looking to Yahweh (1–2\)
2. The servant’s plea: request for mercy (3–4\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Trust

Just as a servant trusts his master to protect him, so the psalmist is trusting God to stop proud people from insulting him. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 123:0

**"I lift up my eyes"**

The psalmist is using **I lift up my eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he looks expectantly toward God for help. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[I look expectantly]

See: Idiom

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 123:1
* **Associated Articles:** Idiom (ID: `33283@UWTranslationManual`)

However, in verse 2, the psalmist shifts to the plural **our** and **us**, indicating that he is now speaking on behalf of a group. If using the singular form of the pronouns here would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural forms in your translation. Alternate translation: \[we lift up our eyes]

## Psalms - Chapter 124 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_zv8z)

Psalm 124 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 124 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Acknowledge Yahweh’s protection from enemies (1–5\)
2. Bless Yahweh who did not let us be destroyed (6–7\)
3. Confess Yahweh as our help and creator (8\)

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Various images for enemies

The psalmist depicts enemies through three different images: devouring beasts (verses 3, 6\), an overwhelming flood (verses 4–5\), and a trapper’s snare (verse 7\). Translators should preserve these distinct images.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 124:0


## Psalms 124:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_t78j)

לוּלֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה שֶׁ⁠הָ֣יָה לָ֑⁠נוּ

**"If not Yahweh who was for us"**

David is making a conditional statement **If not Yahweh**, that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. Yahweh was indeed for Israel, and therefore the disastrous results David goes on to describe did not happen. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: \[If Yahweh had not been on our side]

See: Connect — Contrary to Fact Conditions

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 124:1
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Contrary to Fact Conditions (ID: `33325@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Israel (ID: `person:Israel`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 125 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_sis3)

Psalm 125 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 125 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. This song is also a “psalm of trust,” expressing communal confidence that Yahweh protects his people as permanently as mountains surround Jerusalem. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Those who trust in Yahweh are secure (1–2\)
2. Yahweh preserves the righteous from evil rule (3–5\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh’s protection as surrounding presence

The psalmist pictures Yahweh’s care as physical encirclement, like the hills around Zion. This spatial metaphor may need adaptation where mountains are unfamiliar.

### The righteous and the wicked

The psalm contrasts the righteous with workers of iniquity, promising that evil rule will not persist over God’s allotted land.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 125:0

## Psalms - Chapter 126 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_q9ig)

Psalm 126 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 126 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. This song is a “psalm of praise” for Yahweh bringing captives home. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Rejoice in Yahweh’s past restoration (1–3\)
2. Pray for renewed restoration and blessing (4–6\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Sorrow and joy

People may have sorrow now; but later it will turn into joy. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/other/joy]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 126:0

## Psalms - Chapter 127 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_ipx7)

Psalm 127 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 127 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Recognize the futility of work without Yahweh (1–2\)
2. Receive children as Yahweh’s gift and blessing (3–5\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Blessings

Yahweh wants his people to have rest. It is a blessing to have many children. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### “of Solomon”

The superscription of this psalm is “of Solomon.” This may mean that Solomon wrote this psalm. But it may also mean that someone else wrote this psalm in honor of Solomon. We recommend that you translate the superscription in a way that allows for this possibility as well as for the possibility that Solomon was the author.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 127:0

The point of this comparison is that just as **arrows** in the hand of a warrior are powerful and useful for defense, so **the sons** a man has in his youth can help defend a man from his enemies when he grows old. ## Psalms - Chapter 128 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_f8w6)

Psalm 128 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 128 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Enjoy the fruit of fearing Yahweh (1–4\)
2. Experience peace and prosperity from Yahweh (5–6\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 128:0

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: \[How happy is everyone fearing Yahweh] or \[Truly blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh]

See: Exclamations

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 128:1
* **Associated Articles:** Exclamations (ID: `33270@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms - Chapter 129 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_p9dv)

Psalm 129 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 129 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Recall Israel’s long affliction (1–4\)
2. Trust Yahweh to defeat the enemies of Zion (5–8\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Yahweh saves

Israel’s enemies have always persecuted them but God has saved them from their enemies. He prays that this enemy will be destroyed with no one to wish them well. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/save]])

Translation Issues in This Psalm
--------------------------------

### Israel addressed as a person

The first section of this psalm, verses 1–4, uses first person singular pronouns since the Israelites are asked to speak as a person who is reciting the story of how he has been cruelly treated by his enemies since he was young. This can be seen as the Israelites recitation of Israel’s history as a nation. If it would be more clear in your language you could use plural pronouns in this section.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 129:0


## Psalms 129:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_nj0r)

רַ֭בַּת

**"Abundantly"**

The word translated as **Abundantly** could refer to: (1\) affliction that is frequent. Alternate translation: \[Often] or (2\) affliction that is severe. Alternate translation: \[Severely]

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 129:1

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Israel (ID: `person:Israel`)

## Psalms 129:1 (#2) (id: en_tn_PSA_fc08)

צְרָר֣וּ⁠נִי מִ⁠נְּעוּרַ֑⁠י

**"they have afflicted me from my youth"**

The pronoun **me** here signals that from here through verse 4, people of Israel are speaking together as though they are the nation of Israel. See the discussion in the introduction to this psalm to decide whether your translation will use the plural pronoun forms or keep the singular. Alternate translation: \[they have afflicted us from our youth]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 129:1
* **Associated Articles:** Pronouns — When to Use Them (ID: `33424@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Israel (ID: `person:Israel`)

צְרָר֣וּ⁠נִי

**"they have afflicted me"**

The pronoun **they** does not refer to a specific group of people. It refers generally to the enemies of Israel throughout its history. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that more clearly. Alternate translation: \[my enemies have afflicted me]

See: Pronouns — When to Use Them

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 129:1
* **Associated Articles:** Pronouns — When to Use Them (ID: `33424@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Israel (ID: `person:Israel`)

The psalmist is saying what he wants the people of Israel to say and inviting them to join in communal recitation. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to say. Alternate translation: \[Israel should indeed say]

See: Third\-Person Imperatives

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 129:1

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Israel (ID: `person:Israel`)

## Psalms 129:2 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_tmjr)

גַּ֝ם לֹא־יָ֥כְלוּ לִֽ⁠י

**"however, they did not prevail against me"**

The psalmist uses the word **however** here to indicate a contrast between the repeated affliction described in the first half of the verse and the failure of the enemies to ultimately prevail. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: \[in spite of that, they did not prevail against me]

See: Connect — Contrast Relationship

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 129:2
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Contrast Relationship (ID: `33329@UWTranslationManual`)


## Psalms 129:3 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_htxp)

עַל־גַּ֭בִּ⁠י חָרְשׁ֣וּ חֹרְשִׁ֑ים הֶ֝אֱרִ֗יכוּ ל⁠מענות⁠ם

**"Upon \& plowed; they made long their furrows"**

The psalmist is speaking of the enemies’ oppression as if they were farmers plowing furrows on his back. The image of **the plowers plowed** upon his back and **they made long their furrows** represents severe and prolonged suffering. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: \[They made me suffer, like a farmer plowing a field they made deep wounds in my back]

## Psalms - Chapter 130 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_c2ly)

Psalm 130 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 130 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. It is a “psalm of praise” that God forgives sins. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Cry out to Yahweh from the depths (1–4\)
2. Wait and hope in Yahweh’s redeeming love (5–8\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Forgive

God forgives sin and helps the sinner. So Israel should trust in God for his forgiveness. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 130:0

Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[Because of my many troubles]

## Psalms - Chapter 131 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_yot5)

Psalm 131 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 131 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion. It is a “psalm of trust.” See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Reject pride and self\-exaltation (1\)
2. Rest quietly in Yahweh like a weaned child (2\)
3. Call Israel to hope in Yahweh (3\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### Humility as Contentment

The psalmist expresses humility not as self\-deprecation but as willing acceptance of one’s place before God, refusing to pursue matters beyond his scope.

### The Weaned Child

A weaned child resting on its mother is content without demanding anything. This simile pictures a soul at peace with God, no longer driven by unmet desire.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 131:0


## Psalms 131:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_jzvi)

לֹא־גָבַ֣הּ לִ֭בִּ⁠י וְ⁠לֹא־רָמ֣וּ עֵינַ֑⁠י

**"my heart is not high and my eyes are not raised up"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Both phrases express that David is not proud. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[I am not at all proud, nor do I act arrogantly]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 131:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 131:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 132 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_h7z9)

Psalm 132 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 132 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Remember David’s devotion to Yahweh (1–9\)
2. Affirm Yahweh’s promise to David’s line (10–12\)
3. Celebrate Yahweh’s choice of Zion (13–18\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Psalm
---------------------------------------------

### The Davidic Covenant

Yahweh swore that David’s descendants would reign if they kept his covenant.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 132:0

## Psalms - Chapter 133 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_lg1c)

Psalm 133 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 133 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Celebrate the goodness of unity (1–2\)
2. Declare Yahweh’s blessing where unity dwells (3\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 133:0

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 133:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 134 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_az9r)

Psalm 134 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 134 is one of the songs of ascents (Psalms 120–134\). These are generally understood to be songs that were customarily sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem for one of the three major annual festivals. The term “ascents” is used because going up to the temple in Jerusalem involved a climb up Mount Zion.

1. Call Yahweh’s servants to bless him (1–2\)
2. Receive blessing from Yahweh the creator (3\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 134:0

The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: \[Pay attention]

See: Metaphor

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 134:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metaphor (ID: `33292@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Bless (ID: `keyterm:Bless`); LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`); House (ID: `realia:House`)

## Psalms - Chapter 135 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_qzj7)

Psalm 135 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 135 is a “psalm of praise” focusing on worshiping God because his greatness.

1. Call to praise Yahweh (1–4\)
2. Yahweh’s power over creation and history (5–14\)
3. Idols are worthless but Yahweh is worthy of praise (15–21\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter
-----------------------------------------------

### Praise

The people, priests and their helpers should praise God because he is so great. He defeated the Egyptians and led his people to the promise land. Idols have no power.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 135:0


## Psalms 135:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_d1cp)

הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ

**"Hallelu Yah"**

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: \[Halleluia] or \[Praise Yah]

See: Copy or Borrow Words

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 135:1
* **Associated Articles:** Copy or Borrow Words (ID: `33407@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 135:13 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_d1e2)

יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֣ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֑ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה זִכְרְ⁠ךָ֥ לְ⁠דֹר־וָ⁠דֹֽר

**"Yahweh, your name {is} to forever; Yahweh, your remembrance {is} to generation and generation"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh, you will be known and remembered through every generation] or \[Yahweh, your name is to forever, indeed, your remembrance is to generation and generation]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 135:13
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 136 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_wah2)

Psalm 136 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 136 is a “psalm of thanksgiving.” It is a responsive psalm. One person or group would sing the first part and then the other group would sing the repeated refrain.

1. Give thanks for who Yahweh is (1–3\)
2. Give thanks for Yahweh’s works in creation (4–9\)
3. Give thanks for Yahweh’s acts of deliverance and care (10–26\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter
-----------------------------------------------

### Israel blessed

God has blessed Israel throughout its history and taken care of the needy people. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/kt/bless]])

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 136:0

## Psalms - Chapter 137 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_syg4)

Psalm 137 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 137 is a “psalm of supplication” or “lament.” See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Grief and remembrance in exile (1–4\)
2. Commitment to remember Jerusalem (5–6\)
3. Cry for Yahweh’s justice against enemies (7–9\)

Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter
-----------------------------------------------

### Songs of Zion

The captives are told to sing songs of Zion there in Babylon but they felt too unhappy to want to sing. The army from Babylon was cruel when it destroyed Jerusalem and the people of Edom encouraged them to destroy Jerusalem. They prayed that God will be cruel to the people of Edom and Babylon.

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 137:0

Here, **Zion** represents the temple and the community of God’s people who worshiped there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: \[our homeland]

See: Metonymy

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 137:1
* **Associated Articles:** Metonymy (ID: `33293@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Jerusalem (ID: `place:Jerusalem`); Babylon (ID: `place:Babylon`)

## Psalms 137:4 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_iqoh)

## Psalms 137:5 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_llr1)

אִֽם־אֶשְׁכָּחֵ֥⁠ךְ יְֽרוּשָׁלִָ֗ם תִּשְׁכַּ֥ח יְמִינִֽ⁠י

**"If"**

The psalmist is presenting a possible condition and its consequence. He says that if he forgets Jerusalem, then his right hand should no longer be able to play the harp. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: \[If I forget you, Jerusalem, then let my right hand forget]

## Psalms 137:5 (#3) (id: en_tn_PSA_rqvs)

תִּשְׁכַּ֥ח יְמִינִֽ⁠י

**"QUOTE\_NOT\_FOUND: תִּשְׁכַּ֥ח יְמִינִֽ⁠י"**

The psalmist is using **let my right hand forget** as a common expression of the culture to mean that his hand would lose its ability to play a musical instrument. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: \[let my right hand lose its skill] or \[let my right hand wither]

See: Idiom

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 137:5
* **Associated Articles:** Idiom (ID: `33283@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Jerusalem (ID: `place:Jerusalem`)

## Psalms 137:5 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_rt0g)

תִּשְׁכַּ֥ח יְמִינִֽ⁠י

**"QUOTE\_NOT\_FOUND: תִּשְׁכַּ֥ח יְמִינִֽ⁠י"**

The psalmist is saying what he wants to happen if he breaks his vow. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: \[I desire that my right hand would forget] or \[may my right hand forget]

See: Third\-Person Imperatives

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 137:5

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Jerusalem (ID: `place:Jerusalem`)

## Psalms 137:6 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_h5xb)

תִּדְבַּ֥ק־לְשׁוֹנִ֨⁠י ׀ לְ⁠חִכִּ⁠י֮ אִם־לֹ֪א אֶ֫זְכְּרֵ֥⁠כִי אִם־לֹ֣א אַ֭עֲלֶה אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֑ם עַ֝֗ל רֹ֣אשׁ שִׂמְחָתִֽ⁠י

**"Let my tongue cling to my palate if I do not remember you, if I do not cause Jerusalem to go up above the head of my joy"**

The psalmist is presenting the consequence first and then the condition. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: \[If I fail to remember you, if I do not cause Jerusalem to go up above the head of my joy, then let me tongue cling to my palate]

See: Connect — Hypothetical Conditions

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 137:6
* **Associated Articles:** Connect — Hypothetical Conditions (ID: `33327@UWTranslationManual`)

## Psalms - Chapter 138 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_lv6z)

Psalm 138 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm is a psalm of praise.
 1\. Wholehearted praise (1–3\)
 2\. Global worship (4–6\)
 3\. Confidence in God’s protection (7–8\)

## Psalms - Chapter 139 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_spl6)

Psalm 139 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 139 is a psalm of praise.

1. God knows everything about me (1–6\)
2. God is everywhere with me (7–12\)
3. God formed me wonderfully (8–18\)
4. God’s righteous anger guides me (19–22\)
5. Inviting God’s search (23–24\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 139:0

## Psalms 139:12 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ivn7)

**"Even darkness does not make it dark to you, and the night shines like the day"**

These two phrases **Even darkness does not make it dark to you** and **the night shines like the day** mean basically the same thing. ## Psalms - Chapter 140 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_qi17)

Psalm 140 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 140 is a deliverance psalm. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]])

1. Cry to Yahweh for protection from the wicked (1–5\)
2. Trust Yahweh as defender and refuge (6–8\)
3. Ask Yahweh to judge evil and uphold the righteous (9–13\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 140:0

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Psalm (ID: `keyterm:Psalm`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms 140:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_lsti)

חַלְּצֵ֣⁠נִי יְ֭הוָה מֵ⁠אָדָ֣ם רָ֑ע מֵ⁠אִ֖ישׁ חֲמָסִ֣ים תִּנְצְרֵֽ⁠נִי

**"Rescue me, Yahweh, from an evil man; from a man of violence preserve me"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[Yahweh, rescue me and preserve me from evil, violent people]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms - Chapter 141 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_j6r9)

Psalm 141 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 141 is a “lament.”

1. Ask Yahweh to hear and accept the prayer (1–2\)
2. Pray for purity in speech and actions (3–5\)
3. Trust Yahweh for protection and deliverance (6–10\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 141:0

## Psalms 141:2 (#4) (id: en_tn_PSA_v28f)

**"May my prayer be established {like} incense to your face, a raising of my palms {like} the evening sacrifice"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[May my prayer and my uplifted hands be truly acceptable to you, like a pleasing offering]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms - Chapter 142 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_psy6)

Psalm 142 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 142 is a psalm of deliverance from his enemies. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]])

1. Pour out complaint and trouble to Yahweh (1–4\)
2. Declare Yahweh as refuge and portion (5–7\)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 143 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_tm9v)

Psalm 143 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 143 is a deliverance psalm. The psalmist prays for deliverance from his enemies. (See: \[\[rc://\*/tw/dict/bible/other/deliverer]])

1. Plead for Yahweh’s mercy and not judgment (1–2\)
2. Describe distress and longing for Yahweh (3–6\)
3. Ask Yahweh for guidance, deliverance, and renewal (7–12\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 143:0


## Psalms 143:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_ra9h)

**"Hear my prayer \& listen to my pleas"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[Hear my prayer, Yahweh; yes, listen to my pleas]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms - Chapter 144 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_j9c6)

Psalm 144 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 144 is a specific type of psalm of supplication, a psalm of trust. (See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) The psalmist does not cry out urgently for help. Instead, he begins by saying how reliable and trustworthy Yahweh is. In the rest of the psalm, the psalmist asks for deliverance from his enemies, but this petition is punctuated by confident expressions of praise for Yahweh as the deliverer.

1. Statement of trust (1–4\)
2. Petition (5–8\)
3. Expression of praise (9–10\)
4. Petition (11–14\)
5. Expression of praise (15\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 144:0

בָּ֘ר֤וּךְ יְהוָ֨ה

**"Blessed {be} Yahweh"**

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: \[I bless Yahweh] or \[Let me praise Yahweh]

See: Active or Passive

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 144:1

## Psalms 144:6 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_t3sg)

בְּר֣וֹק בָּ֭רָק וּ⁠תְפִיצֵ֑⁠ם שְׁלַ֥ח חִ֝צֶּ֗י⁠ךָ וּ⁠תְהֻמֵּֽ⁠ם

**"Light lightning and scatter them; send your arrows and rout them"**

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. It would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be unclear in your language, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: \[Light lightning and scatter them; yes, send your arrows and rout them]

See: Parallelism

## Psalms - Chapter 145 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_nm65)

Psalm 145 Introduction
======================

Psalm 145 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 145 is a psalm of praise. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms. But instead of issuing the usual calls to worship, the psalmist states that he and future generations always will worship Yahweh. He makes this statement repeatedly, interspersing it with reasons to worship.

1. Statement of worship (1–7\)
2. Reason to worship: Yahweh is compassionate (8–9\)
3. Statement of worship (10–13\)
4. Reason to worship; Yahweh provides and help and support (14–20\)
5. Statement of worship (21\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 145:0


## Psalms 145:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_dqdo)

אֲרוֹמִמְ⁠ךָ֣ אֱלוֹהַ֣⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ וַ⁠אֲבָרֲכָ֥ה שִׁ֝מְ⁠ךָ֗ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֥ם וָ⁠עֶֽד

**"I will exalt you, my God, the King, and I will bless your name forever and ever"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[I will exalt you, my God, the King, yes, I will bless your name forever and ever]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 145:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** Bless (ID: `keyterm:Bless`); David (ID: `person:David`)

## Psalms - Chapter 146 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_s9dj)

Psalm 146 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 146 is a psalm of praise. The psalmist begins by calling himself to worship Yahweh, and he then gives reasons others to worship him. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship (1–2\)
2. Reason to worship: Yahweh is eternal and powerful (3–6\)
3. Reason to worship: Yahweh helps people in need and in trouble (7–9\)
4. Reason to worship: Yahweh reigns forever (10\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 146:0


## Psalms 146:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_lozl)

הַֽלְלוּ־יָ֡הּ

**"Hallelu Yah"**

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: \[Halleluia] or \[Praise Yah]

See: Copy or Borrow Words

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 146:1
* **Associated Articles:** Copy or Borrow Words (ID: `33407@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms 146:2 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_dyk8)

**"Let me praise Yahweh in my life; let me make music to my God while I yet {am"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[Let me praise Yahweh my God with music for as long as I live]

## Psalms - Chapter 147 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_ji9w)

Psalm 147 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 147 is a psalm of praise. It presents alternating calls to worship and reasons to worship. These reasons include God’s greatness in creating the world, the way he protects his people and provides for them, and the way he gave his people his laws. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship Yahweh (1a)
2. Reason to worship Yahweh (1b–6\)
3. Call to worship Yahweh (7\)
4. Reason to worship Yahweh (8–11\)
5. Call to worship Yahweh (12\)
6. Reason to worship Yahweh (13–20\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 147:0


## Psalms 147:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_d4gi)

הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ

**"Hallelu Yah"**

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: \[Halleluia] or \[Praise Yah]

See: Copy or Borrow Words

## Psalms - Chapter 148 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_ts9v)

Psalm 148 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 148 is a psalm of praise. It presents alternating calls to worship and reasons to worship. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship Yahweh from the heavens (1–4\)
2. Reason to worship Yahweh from the heavens (5–6\)
3. Call to worship Yahweh from the earth (7–12\)
4. Reason to worship Yahweh from the earth (13–14\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 148:0


## Psalms 148:1 (#1) (id: en_tn_PSA_lpnw)

הַֽלְל֣וּ אֶת־יְ֭הוָה מִן־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֑יִם הַֽ֝לְל֗וּ⁠הוּ בַּ⁠מְּרוֹמִֽים

**"Praise Yahweh from the heavens; praise him in the heights"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[Praise Yahweh, all of you who are in the heavens above]

See: Parallelism

* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 148:1
* **Associated Articles:** Parallelism (ID: `33299@UWTranslationManual`)

* **Associated ACAI Concepts:** LORD (ID: `deity:Lord`)

## Psalms - Chapter 149 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_e44u)

Psalm 149 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 149 is a psalm of praise. It first presents a call to worship and a reason for worship. It then presents a call to worship and a purpose for worship, specifically, to help fight his enemies. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship Yahweh (1–3\)
2. Reason to worship Yahweh (4\)
3. Call to worship Yahweh (5–6a)
4. Purpose for worshiping Yahweh (6b–9\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 149:0

## Psalms - Chapter 150 Introduction (id: en_tn_PSA_r7f5)

Psalm 150 Introduction
======================

Structure and Formatting
------------------------

Psalm 150 is a psalm of praise, but instead of presenting calls to worship and reasons to worship as such psalms typically do, it presents a single call to worship. See the discussion of the types of psalms in the introduction to the book of Psalms.

1. Call to worship (1–6\)
* **Associated Passages:** Psalms 150:0

You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: \[Praise Yah, all people]

**"Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in the expanse of his strength"**

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: \[Praise God in his sanctuary and in his mighty heavens]
